userStories.title: Refund policy contradicts the vault: an undisclosed 14-day money-back guarantee
userStories.description: vault/50-business/pricing.md:204-205 states 'Subscriptions: 14-day money-back guarantee on the first subscription invoice only.' No such guarantee appears on either public legal page — src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:80-82 and src/pages/legal/refund.tsx:45-47 both state subscription fees are non-refundable once a billing period has begun. Either the vault is stale, or we are operating a guarantee we do not disclose (or declining one we promised internally). Support and billing decisions are presumably being made against one of these.
acceptanceCriteria: Determine which is authoritative and reconcile — update the vault note or the public policy, in the same commit per the vault same-commit rule.
If the guarantee is real, disclose it at the point of sale, where it is also a conversion asset.
Review the ToS/refund pages alongside the new disclosure copy so the point-of-sale statements and the legal pages agree.
Check the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver (refund.tsx section 4) and chargeback clause (section 5) with counsel while the pages are open.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Legal-docs] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Cheap to resolve and it removes an internal/external inconsistency that would look bad in any enforcement or dispute context. | PARTIAL 2026-08-02 — AC1 RESOLVED by the owner; AC2 does not apply; AC3/AC4 still need counsel. AC1: the vault was wrong and the public pages are authoritative. I put the evidence to the owner rather than guessing, and they chose delete-the-claim. THE EVIDENCE, gathered before asking so the question was cheap: no 14-day money-back guarantee exists anywhere in the codebase — not in constants, not in the Stripe setup, not in the webhook handlers. Refunds are MANUAL admin actions through admin-billing.ts with an MFA step-up. Both public pages say the opposite of the vault (refund.tsx section 3 and terms.tsx: subscription fees non-refundable once a billing period has begun, except where required by law or expressly granted in writing). What DOES exist is a 14-day free TRIAL, which is real, advertised on the landing page and in the plan picker, and is a completely different thing. Two features sharing a number is the most likely origin of a policy nobody agreed to. WHY THIS MATTERED IN A DIRECTION, and it is the part worth keeping: an internal note promising a refund the public pages deny is a promise support might honour case by case. That produces an UNDISCLOSED policy applied inconsistently, which is worse than either answer on its own — worse than not offering it, and worse than offering it openly. AC2 does not apply: there is no guarantee to disclose at the point of sale. The vault section is rewritten to state the three real rules (subscriptions non-refundable, credit packs non-refundable once a grade is generated but credits never expire, billing errors refunded within 60 days), each pointing at the page or constant that owns it, with a callout recording what the claim was and why it was wrong. refund.tsx and terms.tsx are added to the note's code_refs so a change to either now drifts the note. A SECOND CONTRADICTION FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED: terms.tsx says "Unused grading credits DO NOT ROLL OVER and are not refundable". That conflates two different things. Purchased credit packs never expire — constants.ts:384, migration 00037 and 00415 all say so explicitly. The MONTHLY PLAN ALLOWANCE (users.grades_used_this_month) does reset each cycle and genuinely does not roll over. The word "credits" is used for both, so the sentence is true of one and false of the other. It UNDERSTATES what a paying customer gets, so it costs conversion rather than creating legal exposure — but it is still a false statement in the Terms. I did not edit it: AC4 puts these pages under counsel review, and rewriting Terms copy ahead of that trades one unreviewed statement for another. Recorded in the vault note under its own heading so it is not lost, and carried on this story. NOTE ON MY OWN FIRST READING: I initially thought refund.tsx contradicted the vault on credit expiry too. It does not — "credits do not expire INTO A CASH BALANCE" is about cash redemption, and I had read a truncated line. Checked the full sentence before acting. STILL OPEN: AC3 (reconcile the point-of-sale copy with the legal pages — nothing to reconcile now that there is no guarantee, but the credits sentence above is in scope) and AC4 (the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver in refund.tsx section 4 and the chargeback clause in section 5, both needing counsel). | 2026-08-10 AC3's remaining item is now TRACKED rather than described, and the copy is still untouched. THE CONTRADICTION, measured on both sides this time. FIVE product surfaces tell a customer 'credits never expire' - credit-pack-dialog (twice), upgrade-required-dialog, api-overage-card and cancel-subscription-dialog's keep-list. The Terms say 'Unused grading credits do not roll over and are not refundable'. Both use the word 'credits' for two different things: PURCHASED PACKS never expire (constants.ts CREDIT_PACKS, migrations 00037 and 00415 all say so) while the MONTHLY PLAN ALLOWANCE genuinely does reset. So the sentence is true of one and false of the other, and the one it is false about is the one the customer PAID for. It is the point-of-sale-versus-legal-page disagreement AC3 names, with the point of sale outnumbering the Terms five to one. COPY STILL NOT EDITED, and the previous pass's reasoning is why: AC4 has terms.tsx and refund.tsx under counsel review, and rewriting Terms ahead of that trades one unreviewed statement for another. Agreed then and agreed now. WHAT CHANGED IS THAT IT IS NO LONGER A SENTENCE IN A BACKLOG NOTE. NEW src/test/credit-expiry-claims.test.ts makes it a tracked, annotated exception in the KNOWN_GAPS shape the migrations lint already uses - and the shape is the point, because a plain allowlist rots. FOUR PROPERTIES: (1) the FACT is anchored, so the test fails if 'Credits never expire' quietly leaves constants.ts and the whole thing stops meaning anything; (2) the surfaces that say it are DERIVED, not listed; (3) any NEW contradicting statement fails unless someone adds an entry with a reason and an owning story; (4) THE LIST CAN ONLY SHRINK - an entry whose text no longer matches its file FAILS, so when counsel rewrites the sentence the entry must be deleted rather than left describing a problem that no longer exists. That fourth property is the one worth having. An allowlist that outlives its entries stops being a record and becomes a lie about a lie, and it hides the next real regression behind an entry nobody re-reads. FOUR SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: counsel fixing the Terms while the exception is left behind, a NEW page starting to contradict it, the anchoring fact removed from constants.ts, and an exception added with a throwaway reason. STILL passes:false on the same two: AC3's actual reconciliation (the wording, which is counsel's) and AC4 (the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver in refund.tsx section 4 and the chargeback clause in section 5). AC1 and AC2 remain done - the vault was the stale side, there is no guarantee to disclose. VERIFIED: credit-expiry-claims.test.ts 4 passed (new); npx tsc -b clean; eslint 0 errors / 13 warnings; the whole src/test guard suite 896 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: Guided macro capture — framing, distance and lighting for authenticity shots
userStories.description: There is no guided capture for authenticity evidence: no framing overlay, no distance guide, no lighting instruction. iOS uses .builtInWideAngleCamera with no zoom or focus tuning (CameraSession.swift:238), so macro shots depend entirely on the seller's instinct. Authentication tells are only legible at consistent framing and lighting, and inconsistent capture is itself a source of false positives.
acceptanceCriteria: Add per-slot capture guidance: what to photograph, how close, and how to light it, with a framing overlay.
Investigate closer-focus camera configuration on iOS for macro slots.
Provide worked examples of a good vs unusable macro shot for each slot type.
Measure whether guidance actually improves delivered pixel density and gate the rollout on that.
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Capture][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Depends on the macro slots existing first. | 2026-07-31 AC1 DONE (web). New src/lib/macro-capture-guidance.ts: a distance line, a lighting line and a framing tightness per macro slot. The existing photo-profiles hints said WHAT to shoot and nothing about distance or light, which is where macro shots actually fail. LIGHTING ADVICE IS SLOT-SPECIFIC ON PURPOSE, and this is the substantive part: the failure modes are OPPOSITE. A struck serial is visible only by its shadow and needs single-side low-angle light; a glossy care label needs even indirect light or the print blows out. One reusable 'use good light' sentence would have been easier and would not have changed a single photo -- a test asserts the lighting lines are not all identical, because boilerplate would pass every other assertion in the file. Surfaced on BOTH web capture surfaces: the camera dialog gets a dashed framing box over the live preview plus the two lines beneath it (new optional photoType prop), and the FlipDesk uploader -- where the authenticity slots live and there is no camera dialog -- composes them into its per-slot tooltip rather than inventing a new affordance. THE OVERLAY IS SIZED TO BE SATISFIABLE, which is the reviewable judgement: a guide box you can fill and still be told 'move closer' is worse than no box, so the fill fractions are chosen against the US-2136 floors at the US-2135 caps, and a test walks every slot asserting that filling the box delivers more pixels than that slot's own floor -- so raising a floor without revisiting the overlay fails in CI rather than in a seller's hands. The box is decorative only; the capture is still the full frame, so it constrains composition and never the saved pixels. THE COVERAGE TEST IS WHY THIS PAIRS WITH US-2136: every slot the quality gate can reject now has guidance for getting it right, because a gate without guidance is just blame. STILL OPEN: AC2 (closer-focus camera configuration) is iOS and cannot be built in this environment; AC3 (worked good-vs-unusable examples per slot) needs real example imagery, which is design work rather than code; AC4 (gate the rollout on measured pixel-density improvement) needs the per-photo measurement persisted first, which is US-2135 AC3 and blocked on a migration. Verified: tsc -b clean, lint 0 errors, 2912 tests pass, build green.

userStories.title: Per-brand tell depth is 3 brands and 7 tells, all unverified
userStories.description: CANONICAL_TELLS covers exactly three brands (louisvuitton, coach, gucci) with 7 tells total across categories date_code/stamp/hardware/serial/font — every one marked 'seed:brand-authentication-tells (unverified — review in admin)' at confidence 0.5-0.65, against a taxonomy of 11 categories that includes stitching, construction and material. The separate seeded brand_knowledge.authentication_tells rows are legacy {tell, detail} shape, coerced on read to category 'other' with NO redFlag field (brand-authenticity.ts:88-92), so they contribute almost nothing to the contradiction logic that drives the verdict. admin-brand-knowledge.ts is a working curation surface with validateTellsForWrite and is the right place to do this. EXTENDED 2026-07-19: the KB is also ONE-SIDED. Every field models what a GENUINE example looks like — authentication_tells, tag_eras, country_patterns, registered_numbers — and there is no counterfeit-pattern modelling at all: no known fake markers, no superfake characteristics, no record of a specific counterfeit production tell. authentication_tells is a single column marked 'informational' doing double duty for both directions. Combined with seeded content that says 'NEVER auto-authenticate', the KB currently argues against the product it feeds.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrate legacy {tell, detail} rows into the structured shape so they can carry a category and a redFlag and actually affect the verdict.
Expand verified tells to the brands with real submission volume; mark provenance and confidence per tell.
Establish a review workflow so a tell moves from unverified to verified deliberately, with a named source.
Gate: a brand with no verified tells should widen limitations and lower confidence rather than producing a confident verdict from generic reasoning.

Model counterfeit-side knowledge distinctly from genuine-side tells — a known fake marker is a different kind of fact from 'what a real one looks like', and collapsing them into one informational column is why neither drives the verdict.
Reconcile the seeded 'NEVER auto-authenticate' guidance with the shipped product posture (see US-2133) rather than leaving the KB and the product in contradiction.
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Signal][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Expert-dependent. Note the brand KB currently carries authentication_tells, registered_numbers, tag_eras and country_patterns columns across ~150-200 seeded brands — the columns exist, the depth does not. | SCOPED 2026-07-30 from US-2147 (AC1 here is the same work as US-2147 AC5 — carry it here, it is a duplicate there). Corpus measured: 179 legacy payload arrays / 599 individual {tell,detail} entries across the 37 *_brand_knowledge.sql seeds; 0 structured. TWO TRAPS for whoever does AC1. (1) Categories alone are NOT enough and shipping them alone is a REGRESSION: authenticity-coverage.ts:53 isActionableTell treats any non-'other' category as actionable, so a bulk categorization flips all 179 packs inert->actionable, lifts coverageConfidenceCap 0.75 -> 1.0 and empties the limitations disclosure the PURCHASED add-on owes its buyer — with zero new verified facts. AC1 must land WITH the redFlag/verification work (AC2/AC3/AC5), never before it. (2) Most of the 599 are not authentication tells — they are brand-identification, sizing and comping rules ('American Eagle runs LARGE', 'Anthropologie also SELLS other brands', 'PINK IS NOT VICTORIA'S SECRET — comp it separately'). They are all injected into the <<<KNOWN_AUTHENTICATION_TELLS>>> prompt block (ai-authenticity.ts:409-422) told to 'report a finding per tell', against MAX_TELLS 60, so they manufacture noise findings AND can crowd out real tells. So AC1 is a SEPARATION job first: split identification knowledge out of authentication_tells, then categorize only what actually authenticates. That separation likely needs its own column or table, which makes AC1 a migration with a schema change, not a JSONB rewrite. Guard already in place: authenticity-coverage_test.ts:201 fails the moment a structured payload appears. Remains EXPERT-DEPENDENT and unstarted — a genuine redFlag needs a named source, which is AC3's review workflow. | 2026-08-09 AC1 INHERITS A MEASURED WARNING FROM US-2147, transplanted here because US-2147 AC5 is the same requirement verbatim and that story is now closed — leaving the finding only on a closed story is how it gets re-derived the expensive way. THE OBVIOUS VERSION OF AC1 IS A USER-VISIBLE REGRESSION ON A PAID PRODUCT. Measured corpus (2026-07-30): 179 legacy payload arrays holding 599 individual {tell,detail} entries across the 37 *_brand_knowledge.sql seeds; structured payloads = 0. authenticity-coverage.ts:53 isActionableTell returns true when category is not 'other' OR redFlag is set — so ASSIGNING CATEGORIES ALONE flips all 179 packs from inert to actionable, which lifts coverageConfidenceCap from COVERAGE_CAP_INERT 0.75 to 1.0 and empties the limitations string the PURCHASED authenticity add-on owes its buyer. US-2219 shipped that cap precisely because these rows cannot move a verdict. A bulk categorization would therefore raise confidence and delete a disclosure without adding one verified fact — a regression dressed as a data migration. SECOND FINDING, and it reshapes AC1 rather than just cautioning it: MOST OF THE 599 ARE NOT AUTHENTICATION TELLS. The column is doing double duty as general brand knowledge. Real seed entries: 'American Eagle runs LARGE', 'Anthropologie also SELLS other brands', 'PINK IS NOT VICTORIA'S SECRET — comp it separately', 'AERIE IS AMERICAN EAGLE — and the tag does not say so'. All 599 are injected into the KNOWN_AUTHENTICATION_TELLS block (ai-authenticity.ts:409-422) under an instruction to check the item against each. So AC1 is not a shape conversion — it is a TRIAGE: which of the 599 are authentication tells at all, which are sizing/comping facts that belong somewhere else entirely, and only then what category and redFlag the survivors carry. Doing the conversion without the triage moves brand-comping advice into a field the verdict reads as authentication evidence. | 2026-08-09 AC4 SHIPPED. It was a LIVE gap, not a theoretical one: coverage classification asked whether a tell could MOVE a verdict (isActionableTell — does it name a category, does it carry a red flag) and never asked whether anyone had checked the tell is TRUE. So the three brands with structured tells classified as fully covered and took NO confidence cap at all, even though all seven of their tells are sourced to 'seed:brand-authentication-tells (unverified — review in admin)'. A PAID authenticity verdict was riding at full confidence on unreviewed seed data. The existing tests agreed with the bug — four of them failed the moment the fix landed, which is the cleanest evidence the gap was real rather than cosmetic. WHAT SHIPPED: a fourth coverage level, 'unverified', between 'inert' and 'actionable', with COVERAGE_CAP_UNVERIFIED 0.85. NEW isVerifiedTell keys on the 'seed:' source prefix via a NAMED constant now exported from brand-authenticity.ts (UNVERIFIED_SOURCE_PREFIX) rather than a re-typed string literal — that is the convention the module already established, and the US-1715 verify queue's job is to REPLACE the source with a real citation, so 'source still starts with seed:' is exactly the question 'has a human signed this off'. An UNSOURCED tell is also unverified: an unsourced claim is not better than a self-declared draft. THE CAP IS A BAND, NOT A MEASUREMENT, and it is written under the same discipline as the two beside it — the module's own comment refuses a gradient because the golden set (US-2131) has not measured what thin coverage costs. 0.85 sits between 0.75 and 1.0 because an unreviewed structured tell is genuinely more use than a descriptive note (a finding can still be attributed to a category) and genuinely less than a confirmed one, and it does not pretend to know by how much. BOTH CONDITIONS MUST HOLD ON THE SAME TELL, and a test pins it: one verified descriptive note plus one unreviewed structured tell is not a brand we have verified criteria for. Counting them separately would let a pack launder itself to full coverage with two half-qualifying entries. 4 new cases plus 4 existing ones updated to assert the corrected behaviour rather than deleted — the STRUCTURED fixture stays unsourced (which is the real state of every seeded tell) and a VERIFIED fixture was added beside it for the assertions that genuinely meant 'real coverage'. REMAINING ON THIS STORY: AC1 (the legacy triage — see the transplanted warning above; a bulk categorization would flip all 179 packs from inert to actionable, lift the cap and empty a paid disclosure without adding one verified fact, and most of the 599 entries are not authentication tells at all), AC2 and AC3 (sourcing and workflow — content, not code), AC5 (model counterfeit-side knowledge distinctly) and AC6 (reconcile the seeded NEVER-auto-authenticate guidance with the shipped posture). NOTE AC4 GETS STRONGER AS AC1 PROGRESSES rather than weaker: every legacy row that becomes structured now lands in 'unverified' until someone cites it, which is the safe direction. VERIFIED: deno lint + deno check src/main.ts clean, full edge suite 6229 passed / 0 failed, vault:lint --strict clean. | 2026-08-09 (same day, follow-up) CORRECTING A DEFECT I SHIPPED IN THE PREVIOUS COMMIT. Adding the 'unverified' coverage level without giving it its own disclosure branch left it falling through to the INERT wording, which reads 'Our brand-specific criteria for this brand are descriptive notes rather than checkable tests'. THAT IS FALSE AT THIS LEVEL: the criteria ARE checkable tests — nobody has confirmed them. Both surfaces were affected, coverageLimitation (the disclosure on the delivered assessment) and purchaseDisclosure (the one a purchase flow must show before taking money). A WRONG EXPLANATION ON A PAID DISCLOSURE IS WORSE THAN A VAGUE ONE, and that is why this is a defect rather than a polish item: the buyer can ACT on it. They would conclude we hold no real tests for the brand when we hold untested ones, which is a different decision about whether to trust the assessment and whether to inspect the item themselves. Both levels now have their own wording, saying what is actually true — checkable but not yet verified against a cited source. THE GENERAL SHAPE, worth keeping: a confidence cap without a matching disclosure is exactly what this module exists to prevent — the buyer pays, the confidence is quietly lowered, and nothing says why. Adding a cap level is therefore a THREE-part change (classify, cap, disclose) and I shipped two of the three. A new test asserts the invariant directly rather than the instance: every level except 'actionable' owes a non-empty limitation AND a non-null purchase disclosure, and the three texts must all DIFFER — three identical strings would mean the levels are not really distinct to the person reading them, which is the only place the distinction matters. That test would have caught the omission, and it will catch the next one. 3 new cases, 22 in the file. VERIFIED: deno lint + deno check clean, full edge suite 6232 passed / 0 failed. | 2026-08-09 AC6 IS A DUPLICATE OF US-2133 AC3, word for word in substance: 'Reconcile the brand-KB never-auto-authenticate guidance with the shipped product posture.' US-2139 AC6 even says 'see US-2133'. Two stories owning one requirement is the same shape resolved earlier today between US-2147 AC5 and US-2139 AC1 — whichever is picked up second finds it done with no record of who did it, or both do it. US-2133 IS THE OWNER and should keep it: the reconciliation depends on US-2133 AC2 (decide and document the claim posture — assessment-with-limitations versus verification), so doing AC6 first would mean reconciling the KB against a posture nobody has settled. ⚠ AND IT IS EXPLICITLY NOT AGENT WORK. US-2133's own note says, in terms: 'Do not let an agent draft the claim language.' Its AC1 requires review WITH COUNSEL. I am surfacing that here rather than only there, because a future agent reading US-2139 top to bottom would reach AC6, see a documentation task, and start writing legal-adjacent copy without ever opening US-2133. THE CONTRADICTION IS REAL, for whoever does resolve it, and worth stating precisely so the work starts from evidence: 37 seeded brand packs carry prose like 'NEVER label a Coach item authentic — flag anything inconsistent in condition notes only' (00398) and 'LUXURY — never auto-authenticate' (00399), while the shipped pipeline's deriveVerdict emits 'likely_authentic' as one of three verdicts. Those may well be reconcilable — a capped, disclosed 'likely authentic' is not the same act as labelling an item authentic — but that is a claim-language judgement with counsel in it, not an engineering one, and the KB prose is spread across immutable applied migrations, so the reconciliation has to land in the vault rather than by editing the seeds. AC6 is therefore CLOSED HERE as a duplicate; the requirement lives on US-2133 AC3.

userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session. [2026-07-19 AC3 DONE + AC1 GUARD HALF. AC2 NEEDS macOS — story stays open] AC3 was the whole point of the story (a comment is not a mechanism) and is now real: src/test/legal-version-parity.test.ts asserts the THREE-WAY agreement between the edge fallbacks (FALLBACK_TOS_VERSION / FALLBACK_PRIVACY_VERSION), web LEGAL_VERSIONS, and the iOS AuthStore.swift static lets, by parsing each source. Negative-verified by bumping the iOS constant to 2026-09-01 — the guard fails naming all three values. AC1: took the guard option the AC explicitly allows rather than making clients read /api/legal at runtime. A build-time comparison against the live DB is not possible (no DB at build), and the edge FALLBACK constants are the DB-backed sources checked-in form, so this pins what CAN be pinned. Making the clients dynamic remains the stronger fix and is still open. Also asserted the versions are ISO dates: the edge ORDERS versions to decide whether re-acceptance is required, so a free-form string would break that comparison silently. And the parse-succeeded guard is explicit, because comparing null to null would have passed vacuously — it caught a real bug immediately when a heredoc ate the backslashes in my regex and both parsers returned null. AC2 NOT DONE and deliberately not faked: iOS has no re-acceptance gate (never calls /api/legal) while web has legal-gate.tsx. I cannot build or test Swift on Windows, and writing a compliance gate blind is precisely the wrong place for that. A test asserts the gap STILL EXISTS so it flips the moment someone implements it, rather than the story looking complete because the parity guard is green. AuthStore.swift now documents the gap in place. Seventh prose-matching guard failure this session: my new Swift comment names /api/legal, which the absence assertion matched. Comments are stripped now. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00142) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping. | 2026-08-10 ⚠ THE RESIDUAL HOLE THIS STORY DESCRIBED NO LONGER EXISTS, BECAUSE THE WHOLE CAPTURE DOES NOT. The 2026-07-18 note says 'handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version'. It does not record anything. TRACED ACROSS ALL SEVEN DEFINITIONS OF THE FUNCTION: 00001, 00037, 00079 (no legal), 00142 (adds the clickwrap capture - users.tos_accepted_version/privacy_accepted_version plus an append-only legal_acceptances row with method 'signup_clickwrap'), then 00303 CREATE OR REPLACE to add use_case with the block simply not carried forward, and 00379 + 00401 rebased on the truncated body - 00401 says in its own header 'Body is identical to 00379'. The last definition wins, so since 00303 NO EMAIL SIGNUP HAS RECORDED A CLICKWRAP AT ALL. WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT: CREATE OR REPLACE does not warn that a new body dropped a previous migration's additions; both columns are nullable; no test exercises the trigger's SQL; and the db verify lane proves migrations APPLY to a fresh schema without ever signing anyone up (firing this trigger needs a running GoTrue, which that lane does not start). THE SECOND CONSEQUENCE IS THE ONE NOBODY WOULD HAVE FOUND. POST /api/legal/confirm-signup (US-2116 AC4, shipped this month) appends server-observed IP and user-agent evidence BESIDE a clickwrap row and REFUSES rather than inventing one when there is nothing to corroborate. Correct behaviour, pointed at a row that no longer exists - so decideSignupConsentEvidence returns no_signup_clickwrap for every caller and that entire strengthened-evidence path has recorded nothing, ever, on the highest-volume consent path. Its module header, its route comment and 00573's column comment all describe it working. The first consequence is milder than this story feared: a NULL recorded version never meets the gate's bar, so legal-gate.tsx fires on first authenticated session and consent IS captured - later, and stamped with whatever is current then. FIXED IN MIGRATION 00586 (HELD - see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md). CREATE OR REPLACE restoring the block onto 00401's body. The inherited half was DIFFED line-by-line against 00401 rather than retyped, and that diff is reported in the commit: the only lines that differ are the ones that had to. AND IT CLOSES AC1's DURABLE HALF, which is why this belongs here rather than in a new story. The AC's stated durable fix was 'the server stamps the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata'. 00142 stamped raw_user_meta_data->>'tos_version' - the browser's hardcoded LEGAL_VERSIONS constant, which is precisely what this story is about. 00586 uses the metadata's PRESENCE as the signal that a clickwrap happened (an OAuth signup sends none and must stay NULL or the gate would never prompt them) and reads the VALUE from legal_documents, ordered exactly as deriveKind() does. accepted_at is now() rather than the client's legal_accepted_at, for the same reason signup-consent-evidence.ts refuses a client-supplied IP: a forgeable value on a consent record is worse than an absent one. NO BACKFILL, DELIBERATELY. Accounts created between 00303 and 00586 have no clickwrap row and cannot get one - the acceptance they gave was never recorded, and writing a row now would be a fabricated consent record with a manufactured timestamp. They are covered by whatever the gate captured on first sign-in. GUARD: NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/legal-acceptance-trigger_test.ts reads the LAST definition of handle_new_user on disk and fails if the clickwrap block is not in it. Negative-verified the only way that matters - moving 00586 out of the directory reddens all five cases, i.e. the guard fails against the state the repo was ACTUALLY in. TWO SABOTAGES PASSED FIRST AND THE FIX GENERALISES. My assertions read the whole migration FILE, and the file's own header explains what the function does using the same identifiers - so renaming the method string to signup_clickwrap_v2 and drifting the ORDER BY both left the prose matching and the guard green. Every assertion now reads the body from the CREATE onward. Two more passed because the trigger does each lookup TWICE (tos and privacy) and I mutated only the first; the ORDER BY and fallback checks are now COUNTED at 2. That is the third and fourth time today a guard has checked that the code says the right thing somewhere rather than in the place that matters. VAULT: NEW vault/20-domain/signup-consent-capture.md, and it is not optional decoration - vault-lint FAILED the commit because the migration header ran to 54 lines, over the US-2059 knowledge limit. That rule is exactly right here: an applied migration is immutable, so a regression history left in its header could never be corrected. The note carries the four acceptance methods, the server-resolved-version rule, the ORDER BY mirror, and the standing rule that any future replacement of handle_new_user must be DIFFED against the previous definition rather than written fresh. The header now points at it. STILL passes:false. AC2 (an iOS re-acceptance gate) is unchanged and needs macOS - iOS still never calls /api/legal. AC1's other half (clients reading the version at runtime instead of a build-time parity guard) is also unchanged; what landed is the SERVER-side stamp, which is the half that decides what gets recorded. ⚠ NOT EXECUTED. Docker was down, so scripts/verify.mjs --db could not boot the throwaway stack and this SQL has never been run against a Postgres. What WAS checked: the inherited body diffed against 00401, the INSERT column and value lists counted (15 each), and every column written confirmed against 00142's CREATE TABLE. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md says this plainly and marks the risk MEDIUM - the function runs on every signup, though a parse failure at apply time leaves 00401's definition in place, which is today's state and therefore safe. VERIFIED: EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped to 00586 in the same commit, manifest regenerated (331 footer-era migrations), self-record footer present; migrations-lint clean (584 migrations, 5 annotated gaps); full edge suite 6439 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 5); deno lint clean across 1483 files; deno check src/main.ts 0 errors; npx tsc -b clean; eslint 0 errors / 13 warnings; vault:lint --strict clean (165 notes). SEVEN SABOTAGE MUTATIONS after the fixes, each reddening its own named case: 00586 removed entirely, the audit-row insert dropped in a 00303-shaped edit, the version taken from the browser again, the method string drifted, the ORDER BY drifted, the fallback drifted, and an OAuth signup stamped.

userStories.title: Grading determinism (US-481) is void on the default model, and the code still claims it
userStories.description: ai-config.ts:157-179 documents that grading ALWAYS uses a low temperature, defaulting to 0 (fully greedy decoding), because a certified score backs a public 'standardized' value prop. But gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort — not temperature — for effort-based models, and the default grading model (DEFAULTS.model = claude-sonnet-5) is effort-based. So getGradingTemperature() is never called on the shipping path, GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE and the whole clamping apparatus are dead code, and grading runs at the model's own non-greedy decoding. A regrade of the same photos can return a different score with no explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE the product position: is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? That is a trust question, not an engineering one.
If determinism is still the promise: add a self-consistency check (grade twice, compare, flag divergence) or pin a decoding mode that guarantees it.

If it is NOT the promise: correct the ai-config.ts comment block, which currently asserts a property the code does not have, and disclose run-to-run variance wherever the 'standardized grade' claim is made.
Either way the comment must stop describing temperature clamping as though it governs grading.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. I VERIFIED the mechanism myself: DEFAULTS.model is claude-sonnet-5 (ai-config.ts:12), modelUsesEffort() matches it (:189-192), and gradingSamplingParams() returns the effort branch with no temperature (:228-233). This is NOT a code bug — effort-based models do not accept temperature, so the US-1033 migration was a correct API fix. The defect is that it silently removed a DOCUMENTED GUARANTEE and nobody updated the guarantee. Code that claims a property it no longer has is the most dangerous state for a trust product, because everyone downstream reasons from the claim rather than the behaviour. I deliberately did not 'fix' it: the right answer is a product decision — restore determinism (costly, possibly not available on this model family) or stop promising it (cheap, but it changes what a certificate means). [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC3(a)+AC4 DONE, AC1/AC2/AC3(b) BLOCKED ON A PRODUCT DECISION] Verified the technical claim in full: getDefaultModel()=claude-sonnet-5 is effort-based, so gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort and NO temperature; getGradingTemperature()/GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE are dead on the shipping path. Found a THIRD layer the story did not name: grading-reliability.ts implements the self-consistency math AC2 asks for, is pure and tested, but has ZERO non-test callers — the env-gated live-sampling job it describes was never built. So the determinism promise is unenforced at every level: no greedy decoding, no measurement, no gate. Done: both false comment blocks (ai-config.ts, grading-reliability.ts) now describe reality and name the open decision; new src/tests/grading-determinism_test.ts pins the actual behaviour (4 tests) so the claim cannot silently drift back. BLOCKED: AC1 is explicitly a trust/product call — is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? AC2 depends on that answer (wire grading-reliability.ts as a live self-consistency gate vs accept variance); AC3(b) public-copy disclosure depends on it too. userStories.notes: [P2][GEO/Authority] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. The story says no tolerance language exists anywhere; true of grading-scale.ts/grade-standard.ts, but defect-weighting.ts has carried REAL measurable data since US-1028 — physical size buckets in mm (pinhole <3mm, small 3-13mm, medium 13-50mm, large >50mm), SEVERITY_MULT, and a full FACTOR_ROUTING defect->factor table. New src/lib/grading-standard.ts mirrors the engine (frontend cannot import from services/edge-functions) and grading-standard-parity.test.ts guards every mirrored value, including that unknown size stays <= small so missing data never inflates a penalty. DELIBERATE OMISSION: BASE_WEIGHT (exact score-points penalty per defect type) is NOT published. Publishing which factor a flaw hits makes the standard auditable; publishing the exact penalty makes it gameable — a seller who knows the arithmetic photographs to minimise it. A test asserts it stays out. Reversing that is a product call. AC5 read like a process footnote and is actually the load-bearing one: publishing engine criteria CHANGED WHAT A CHANGE TO THEM MEANS, and nothing recorded that. So the natural next edit is a private calibration tweak that silently makes a published spec wrong. userStories.notes: [P2][Growth/Experimentation] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Pairs with US-2101 (UTM capture) — together they make conversion work measurable rather than anecdotal. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC2+AC4 DONE; AC3 (one real experiment) DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The connector exists: src/lib/client-experiments.ts (logic, testable without React) + src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts (subscription plumbing), returning {variant, ready}. The story called it a connector not a framework and that was right — this layer does NO bucketing, rollout or targeting, because PostHog already does all three. THREE INTEGRITY PROPERTIES, each of which is the difference between an experiment that reports a number and one whose number is true. (1) CONSENT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CHECKED: flags are read off window.posthog, which analytics.ts only creates after opt-in, so there is no code path that can bucket an unconsented visitor — nothing exists to ask. AC2 is satisfied by construction rather than by a guard someone can forget. (2) NO MID-SESSION FLIPS: a resolved variant is LOCKED for the page session. PostHog re-delivers flags on identify and on payload refresh, and a paywall whose copy changes mid-read gives you a visitor who saw BOTH arms and belongs to neither. (3) EXPOSURE IS AN EVENT, NOT AN EVALUATION: experiment_exposed fires once per flag per session and only when the caller says the variant was actually SHOWN — the hook takes an `exposed` argument for surfaces that mount before they are visible. Analysing on $feature_flag_called (which fires when code merely ASKS) is the standard way a real effect gets diluted into a tie. THE SUBTLEST DECISION: undefined from getFeatureFlag is kept SEPARABLE from an actual control rather than collapsed into it. They look identical — both render control — but collapsing them counts every visitor into the control arm during the flag-load window, which makes a winning experiment read as a tie. That is why the return is {variant, ready} and not just a string. 13 tests. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three properties by simulating the careless edit: dropping the lock reddens 2, dropping the exposure resolution-guard reddens 1, collapsing undefined into control reddens 3; restoring returns to green. AC4 DONE as vault/40-growth/experimentation.md (contract) — and writing it surfaced a REAL FINDING the story did not anticipate: the Experiments Governor (US-1609) has adapters for the four server-side engines and NONE for client-side, so a paywall test is invisible to its interference detection and could run against the same conversion metric as a drip test with both reads looking clean. Recorded as a warning callout with the manual check to do meanwhile. Also noted: the consent category model has no vault note, which is a gap. AC3 NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: there is no web paywall component (paywall is iOS/Android), so the named surface is the pricing page, and choosing what to test there means authoring alternative pricing copy/layout — a product and design decision, not a code one. The mechanism is ready and wiring a chosen variant is now a small edit. Verified: 2462 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, vault:lint clean (3 drift warnings pre-existing from earlier commits today, not from this work).

Corroborating: the live cert page renders 'Certificate No. GT-7Y3BCAF', proving grade_reports.certificate_number (00307) is selectable and the US-1945 genesis-only drift fallback is NOT being hit. SHIPPED THIS PASS: /health/ready now reports { schema: { expected, applied, status } }. Drift was previously visible ONLY in container logs, which is exactly how this story's premise went 130 migrations stale without anyone noticing it had been fixed — nothing served the answer. Now a curl distinguishes match / ahead / behind / unknown, and 'unknown' names the residual case above explicitly. Drift deliberately does NOT flip `ready`: behind is already fatal at boot, and AHEAD is the NORMAL state in the migrate-then-deploy order this repo mandates, so gating readiness on it would pull healthy containers from rotation during every correct deploy. 5 new tests in health_test.ts (incl. an explicit assertion that drift never affects the ready decision, and that the schema block is omitted for existing 3-arg callers). The four that first looked orphaned (ACCESS_KEY_ID, SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, DEV_ID, VERIFICATION_TOKEN) are a slash-shorthand in the table — 'SES_AWS_REGION/ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' and 'EBAY_APP_ID/CERT_ID/DEV_ID/VERIFICATION_TOKEN' — and the expanded forms all exist (SES_AWS_* in lib/email-transport.ts, EBAY_CERT_ID and EBAY_DEV_ID in lib/ebay-client.ts, EBAY_VERIFICATION_TOKEN in lib/ebay-notification-subscriptions.ts). So an operator working this checklist will not set a name nothing reads — worth knowing before the prod session, since that failure mode is silent: the box gets ticked and the feature stays dark. The document is correct, and a checker would need slash-shorthand expansion to avoid flagging correct prose — the same false-positive trap that made me fix the doc-refs guard to resolve contextual roots. userStories.notes: 2026-08-02 AC1 DONE; AC2 and AC3 recorded as blocked with the reason, not attempted. AC1: measure-card.tsx gains a "Measure an item" card with a primary CTA into /dashboard/flipdesk/inventory?status=cataloged. THE DIAGNOSIS BEHIND THE FIX, because the story's title undersells it: every control on that page produced an ARTEFACT — a PDF to print, a card to be mailed — and not one of them led to the thing the artefact is FOR. A seller who read the whole page still had to already know that measuring happens on an item, and where to find one. That is the specific shape of "brochure": not missing content, missing a next step. TWO CHOICES IN THE LINK WORTH STATING. It points at ?status=cataloged rather than the inventory root, so the seller lands on pre-listed items — the set that actually needs measuring — instead of their entire catalog; statusParamToTab folds cataloged / measured / photographed into the To-list tab, so one status param reaches the right view. And it uses ?status= rather than ?tab= deliberately: status is the documented EXTERNAL entry point that the Overview pipeline grid and the Kanban "+N more" links already use, tab is the table's internal view key, and the mapping function exists precisely so external links survive a tab rename. AC2 NOT DONE — it asks for a before/after sample of a finished buyer-facing measurements photo. That is an image asset. Producing it needs the measure pipeline run against a real garment with a real card in frame, and a judgement about whose item is safe to show publicly. Same class as US-1949 AC1: a human with the product open, not a code change. AC3 NOT DONE, and it splits. The TRACKING NUMBER half needs a schema change: measure_card_requests (00351) has status, requested_at, shipped_at and card_version, and NO tracking column — so there is nothing to render, and adding one is a migration plus a fulfilment-side write that nothing currently produces. The ETA half could be rendered without a migration from status + requested_at, but only if a real fulfilment SLA exists to quote; inventing "ships in 3-5 days" on a page a paying seller reads is a promise the system does not make. Both need an answer about the fulfilment process before they are code. VERIFIED: build clean through the 216-route prerender, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, 100 flipdesk tests pass. | 2026-08-08 AC3's TRACKING HALF DONE. AC2 and AC3's ETA half stay open, both for the reasons the previous note gave and neither has changed. The previous pass split AC3 correctly and I built the half that was buildable. NEW migration 00561_measure_card_tracking.sql adds tracking_number and tracking_carrier to measure_card_requests; the operator queue can record them on the shipped transition, and the seller's own /card-request read returns them. BOTH COLUMNS ARE NULLABLE, and that is the design rather than laziness: cards are mailed by hand and many go out as untracked letters. NOT NULL would either stop the operator marking those shipped at all or push them to type a placeholder, and a PLACEHOLDER TRACKING NUMBER IS WORSE THAN AN EMPTY ONE, because the seller clicks it. The route never writes an empty string for the same reason - a test forbids the `tracking || ""` fallback specifically. THE REFUSAL THAT MATTERS, and the reason this needed more than a column. The bulk status route takes up to 500 ids; tracking is per-PARCEL. Sending a number with a batch would stamp ONE carrier reference onto every seller in it, and each would then see a link tracking somebody else's parcel - worse than no tracking, because it looks authoritative. The route refuses it (400) rather than trusting the caller, and refuses tracking on the 'exported' transition too, which would record a parcel that has not been sent. PLAINTEXT, DECIDED NOT DEFAULTED. US-2417 (same session) encrypts ship_name/address_line1/ address_line2/city/postal_code on this exact table because they say where a person lives. A tracking number is a carrier's identifier for a parcel, the operator must search and paste it, and it is the one field on the row the SELLER is meant to read back. Same reasoning that keeps state and country readable there. A GUARD AGAINST AN INTERACTION I WOULD OTHERWISE HAVE MISSED: the seller summary has deliberately never echoed the address (US-1579), and since US-2417 those columns are ciphertext - so adding a field to that summary is now a place where a careless change would BOTH undo a privacy decision and return unreadable data. A test asserts the summary still omits ship_name, address_line1 and postal_code. 4 cases in NEW src/tests/measure-card-tracking_test.ts, comments stripped before every assertion. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: the batch guard removed, the shipped-only guard removed, and the empty-string fallback introduced. Each reddened with its own message; route restored and re-run green. VERIFIED: migration applied from clean AND re-applied (idempotent), EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped to 00561 with the manifest regenerated in the same pass, deno check + deno lint clean across 1426 files, full edge suite 6003 passed / 0 failed. 00561 is HELD and packaged in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md with the apply-before-edge-deploy direction: the edge SELECTs both columns by name, so an edge-first deploy answers 42703 and breaks the MeasureCard panel for EVERY seller, not just those with tracking. | 2026-08-09 STATUS CORRECTION — THE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM IN THIS STORY'S NOTES IS STALE. Migrations 00351 and 00561 are both on origin/main (00351 in 16b36508, 00561 in 6a49be11) and applied. Nothing about this story is blocked on a frozen branch. Recorded because prd-lint has been WARNING about exactly this for some time — 'story(ies) still describe a migration as HELD that is already on origin/main' — and the warning went unactioned, which is how a note that says the branch is frozen keeps costing the next reader a session. It cost me one today on two sibling stories with the identical shape (US-2213 and US-2215, both since corrected). A held migration is by definition UNPUSHED; once it lands on origin the word is not merely out of date, it is an active instruction to stop. WHAT IS ACTUALLY OPEN is unchanged and unrelated to migrations: AC2, and the ETA half of AC3. Read the 2026-08-08 note for those. NOTE FOR WHOEVER ADDS THE NEXT HELD MIGRATION: the discipline that works is to write 'HELD' in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md, which is the file that gets emptied on apply, and to reference it from the story rather than restating the status in prose that nobody revisits. Nine migrations are held RIGHT NOW (00564-00572) and they are tracked there, not here.

userStories.title: iOS: the item's own columns don't own their eBay specifics, so changing Size edits nothing the listing will publish
userStories.description: As a seller on iPhone, I want changing Size or Color on the item to update the eBay item specific too, so that I don't have to open Category & Specifics and type the same value a second time.
acceptanceCriteria: Changing a structured column (brand/size/color/material/style) on the iOS item editor updates that column's eBay aspect even when the aspect's provenance is ai_extracted or manual. Today InventoryAspectSync.reassertDerivedAspects builds a 'preserve' map of every manual/aiExtracted aspect and passes it as 'known', so the AI-filled Size survives and the seller's new Size is discarded - the opposite of the documented contract that the columns OWN those five aspects (see the web helper projectColumnAspects in src/lib/ebay-prefill.ts and its tests).

The save writes BOTH aspect stores, not just one: inventory_items.ebay_aspects (+ebay_aspect_sources) AND listings.item_specifics_override (+item_specifics_sources) for this item's listing row. Today the save-time path writes only the inventory_items pair; item_specifics_override is written ONLY by SpecificsEditorModel (the Category & Specifics editor), which is exactly why the seller has to go there for the change to stick - it is the copy publish/revise reads FIRST.

The projection runs even when the item has no eBay category selected yet. Today reassertDerivedAspects returns early on a blank ebay_category_id, so column values set before a category is picked never reach the aspect stores.

The projection is a PURE local function (a Swift mirror of projectColumnAspects: non-empty column overwrites its aspect and stamps provenance inventory_derived; a blanked column clears it), not a server round trip. Today every save calls EbayAspectsService.deriveAspects, so a save costs a network call and a transient failure silently no-ops via try?.

An XCTest asserts the three rules directly: an ai_extracted Size aspect IS overwritten by a changed Size column; a non-column aspect (e.g. Department, Pattern) is left untouched; and a cleared column clears its aspect.

A deno or vitest drift guard asserts the iOS column-to-aspect name mapping matches the web/edge registry (services/edge-functions/src/lib/aspect-registry.ts, vendored to src/lib/ebay-aspect-registry.json), so the two platforms cannot disagree on which aspect a column owns.

Publish still re-normalizes against the real category spec server-side (forceColumnAspects / COLUMN_ASPECT_FALLBACK in flipdesk-ebay.ts), so a raw column value outside eBay's allowed list is still corrected at publish - this story does not change that.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-03 WARNING, READ BEFORE IMPLEMENTING: AC4 and AC5 as written would re-open a bug fixed on 2026-08-02 (commit ea9e27a2). AC4 says to mirror projectColumnAspects, which was DELETED on 2026-08-01. Its replacement, projectColumnAspectsForSpec in src/lib/ebay-prefill.ts, is deliberately OVERWRITE-ONLY: a blank column no longer clears its aspect, because a blank column cannot be told apart from a never-populated one. Clearing is allowed ONLY on a surface that owns the column inputs, which the iOS item editor does, so clear-on-blank inside the iOS EDITOR is fine. What is NOT fine is AC2 combined with AC4: writing a clear-on-blank projection straight into listings.item_specifics_override, the store the publish check reads FIRST. A blank Brand column carrying an AI- or hand-typed Brand aspect is the ordinary state of an iOS-created item, and deleting it there is exactly the reported failure: Brand plainly visible in the specifics editor while publish refuses with "Fill required eBay specifics in the composer: Brand". Also add the reverse pass (reverseProjectAspectColumns) BEFORE the forward one, or a specifics edit typed on iOS is clobbered by the stale column. Read vault/20-domain/sync-source-of-truth.md first; it is the contract.

userStories.title: Lock down SECURITY DEFINER functions: revoke EXECUTE from PUBLIC across public schema
userStories.description: Postgres grants EXECUTE on every new function to PUBLIC by default. No migration in supabase/migrations/ ever revokes it, and no `REVOKE ... ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC` exists anywhere. Because these functions are SECURITY DEFINER they run as the owner and bypass RLS, so any holder of the anon key can call them directly through PostgREST. grant_grade_credits and debit_grade_credits carry no GRANT/REVOKE statements at all; the revenue-dashboard functions (00215_revenue_dashboard.sql:273-274) grant to authenticated and service_role but never revoke the implicit PUBLIC grant. Impact: mint yourself unlimited grade credits, drain another user's credit balance, and read the full revenue and customer roster anonymously.
acceptanceCriteria: New migration revokes EXECUTE on all existing public-schema functions from PUBLIC, then re-grants explicitly to the roles each function actually needs.
`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC` so future functions are closed by default.
Every SECURITY DEFINER function is inventoried with its intended caller role; credit-mutating functions (grant_grade_credits, debit_grade_credits, refund/reserve variants) are service_role only.
A test or CI check fails if a new SECURITY DEFINER function ships without an explicit grant block.
Migration triple honoured: idempotent SQL, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in the same commit, self-record footer.
Run `SELECT proname, proacl FROM pg_proc WHERE pronamespace='public'::regnamespace AND prosecdef;` against prod before and after and record both in the story.
userStories.notes: [P0][Security/DB] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] VERIFIED directly against the code in this session. Pairs with the guard_users_protected_columns gap — either one alone gives free grading. Fix both together. | 2026-08-04 BLOCKED on US-2403, with the migration WRITTEN AND VERIFIED. Two findings, and the first one means the fix as the story describes it would have done NOTHING. (1) THE STORY'S DIAGNOSIS IS HALF WRONG. It says Postgres grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default and no migration revokes it. Reading pg_proc.proacl on a live stack says otherwise: grant_grade_credits carries {postgres=X/postgres, anon=X/postgres, authenticated=X/postgres, service_role=X/postgres} — DIRECT grants to anon and authenticated, granted by postgres, from Supabase's own ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES bootstrap (confirmed in pg_default_acl for both postgres and supabase_admin on schema public, objtype 'f'). PUBLIC does not appear in the ACL at all. So 'REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM PUBLIC' is a NO-OP on exactly the functions the story names. I wrote that version first, applied it, and measured: grant_grade_credits/debit_grade_credits/revenue_dashboard still showed anon_can=t. A migration that looks like a security fix and changes nothing is worse than none, and the only reason I caught it is that I queried the ACLs instead of trusting the revoke. (2) THE CORRECTED MIGRATION IS WRITTEN AND PASSES EVERY CHECK, and is parked at supabase/migrations/00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED (the suffix is deliberate — apply-prod-migrations.sh globs *.sql, so the rename is what stops an accidental apply). It revokes EXECUTE from PUBLIC, anon AND authenticated on every non-extension function in public, closes the ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES that keeps re-granting them, grants service_role everything (the edge calls 48), and then REPLAYS the grants migrations actually made — 43 names for authenticated, 4 for anon, PARSED out of every GRANT EXECUTE statement in the corpus minus any later explicit REVOKE, not authored by judgement. Plus is_admin/is_super_admin/is_reviewer_or_admin explicitly, because a function called inside an RLS policy runs as the QUERYING role and is_admin appears in 29 migrations' policies while having NEVER had a grant — it worked only on the default this removes. Extension functions are excluded via pg_depend deptype 'e' so pg_trgm (installed into public by 00224) keeps its operators. MEASURED AFTER APPLYING, on a fresh stack: all 527 apply from zero; ZERO of the 28 client-callable RPCs (parsed from src/ + ios/ call sites) lost authenticated EXECUTE; grant_grade_credits, debit_grade_credits, grant_api_credits, admin_adjust_credits, revoke_grade_credits and reserve_ai_action are now f/f/t (anon no, authenticated no, service_role yes); revenue_dashboard and system_health keep authenticated because their own migrations explicitly granted it, and lose anon; similarity/show_trgm still callable by PUBLIC. (3) WHY IT IS NOT SHIPPING: verifying the behaviour crashed the database. On this image any function-permission denial for a role in supautils.hint_roles (anon, authenticated, service_role) segfaults the backend. Filed as US-2403 with the isolation. 00527 does not cause it — refund_grade has been revoked since 00048 and crashes identically — but it would take the crashable surface from a handful of RPCs to ~80. REMAINING ACs when unblocked: AC4 (a CI check that a new SECURITY DEFINER function ships with an explicit grant block) is NOT written; AC6 (proname/proacl before and after against PROD) is an operator read. | 2026-08-08 AC4 DONE. AC1/AC2/AC3/AC5 stay parked in 00527_...sql.BLOCKED behind US-2403; AC6 is an operator read against prod. AC4 was the half that never needed either, and it is now written: NEW src/test/security-definer-grants.test.ts. WHAT IT ENFORCES: every CALLABLE SECURITY DEFINER function in the migration corpus must be named by an explicit GRANT EXECUTE or REVOKE somewhere. Silence is not 'closed' on this stack - it is 'open to anon and authenticated', per the pg_proc.proacl reading in the note above - so a function that states nothing has been granted to the browser by a default nobody wrote down, on the one construct in the schema that deliberately bypasses RLS. TRIGGER FUNCTIONS ARE EXEMPT, and that is a real distinction, not a convenience: a RETURNS trigger function is invoked by the trigger machinery as part of the firing statement and EXECUTE is never consulted. 15 of the 83 are that shape. MY OWN FIRST PARSER PRODUCED EXACTLY THE MISCLASSIFICATION THE TEST EXISTS TO PREVENT, and the guard-the-guard is what caught it. Draft one read a fixed 2500-character window after each CREATE FUNCTION. From grant_grade_credits (00037:180) that window runs straight into handle_new_user (00037:233), whose RETURNS TRIGGER made a CREDIT-GRANTING RPC read as an exempt trigger function - so the single function US-2282 had measured carrying EXECUTE for anon on a live database would have been waved through by its own guard. Fixed by bounding each definition at the NEXT CREATE FUNCTION rather than by a character count. Two landmark assertions (a known callable, two known triggers) are what failed; without them the file would have shipped green and wrong. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE COUNTS THAT ONLY THE FIXED PARSER COULD SHOW: 83 distinct SECURITY DEFINER functions, not 86, and 15 trigger functions, not 19 - the extra 4 were non-SECURITY-DEFINER helpers (set_updated_at among them) swept up by the bleeding window. THE DEBT IS ENUMERATED, NOT TOLERATED: 18 callable SECURITY DEFINER functions say nothing about who may execute them. Seven move money or credits (grant_grade_credits, grant_api_credits, debit_api_credits, grant_appstore_credits, grant_buyer_reward_credit, issue_buyer_reward_credit, redeem_buyer_reward_credit) and three are the RLS predicates themselves (is_admin, is_reviewer_or_admin, is_super_admin) - which is the sharper problem, because a function called inside an RLS policy runs as the QUERYING role, so is_admin has always worked ONLY because of the default this debt describes, and hand-revoking it would break 29 migrations' policies at once. That is what 00527 handles as one atomic replay; the list says so, so nobody picks these off one at a time. The list is SHRINK-ONLY in both directions: a name that gains a grant or revoke FAILS the test until its entry is deleted in the same commit, and a name that stops being a SECURITY DEFINER function fails too. So the ground gained cannot be quietly given back, and the list cannot rot into a place where things go to be forgotten. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS with a throwaway migration: a new ungranted callable SECURITY DEFINER function reddened naming it; the SAME function with a REVOKE + GRANT block passed; and granting an existing debt entry reddened the shrink-only case telling the reader to delete the entry. Probe migration removed, tree confirmed clean. VERIFIED: npx tsc -b clean, eslint clean, the three cases pass, full vitest 3671 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: extension.pem private key is committed to the repository
userStories.description: git ls-files confirms extension.pem and extension.crx are tracked. extension.pem begins with `-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----`. .gitignore has no .pem or .crx rule. The key was added 2026-07-13 in commit e1dbc4da; gitleaks failed that commit and every run since has been green because push-mode only scans new commits. This is the Chrome Web Store signing identity for the extension. Anyone with repo read access can publish an update that every installed user auto-receives. Also tracked and probably unwanted: ios-screenshots/Payment/ios.zip, ios-screenshots/screenshots-appstore.zip, ios-screenshots/screenshots-raw.zip.
acceptanceCriteria: Rotate the Chrome Web Store extension key first. Removing the file does not un-leak it.
git rm --cached extension.pem extension.crx; add *.pem, *.crx and ios-screenshots/*.zip to .gitignore.
Decide and record whether git history is rewritten (BFG / filter-repo) or the key is simply treated as burned. Rewriting rewrites every open PR.
gitleaks runs in full-history mode at least once in CI (scheduled, not per-push) so an existing leak is not permanently invisible.
The rotated key is stored where the team's other signing secrets live; the location is named in the runbook, never the value.
userStories.notes: [P0][Security/Secrets] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] VERIFIED directly against the code in this session. via git ls-files + file header + .gitignore read. Rotation is a human action, not a code change. | PARTIAL 2026-08-01 — the code half is done; AC1 (rotate) and AC3 (the rewrite-or-burn decision) are HUMAN actions and are now written down where the person doing them will find them. AC2 DONE: extension.pem, extension.crx and the three ios-screenshots zips are untracked via git rm --cached, and .gitignore refuses *.pem, *.crx, *.p12, *.keystore, *.jks and ios-screenshots/**/*.zip — broader than the story asked because the next leak will not be another .pem. Verified with git check-ignore. AC4 DONE: NEW .github/workflows/secret-scan-history.yml runs gitleaks over the FULL history weekly (Mondays 06:00 UTC, plus workflow_dispatch), with fetch-depth:0 and the gitleaks BINARY rather than gitleaks-action — the action derives its scan scope from the triggering event and on a schedule there is no diff, so `detect` over the checked-out repo is the unambiguous form. The report uploads on failure, because a bare red X names nothing. WHY THIS IS THE ACTUAL DEFECT and worth stating plainly: there WAS a secret scanner, it WAS working, and it could not have caught this. secret-scan.yml runs in push/PR mode, which scans the commits in the triggering event; it failed the commit that added the key on 2026-07-13 and every run after that was green while the key sat in history. Per-push asks 'is this change clean?'; only a history sweep asks 'is the repository clean?'. AC5 DONE (structurally): vault/10-ops/key-rotation.md gains a section for this key — what it grants (publish an update EVERY installed user auto-receives, i.e. code execution in their browsers, not read access to something), the rotation steps, and an explicit blank line for the storage location, left blank rather than guessed at because naming the wrong vault entry is worse than naming none. AC3 is RECORDED not decided: both options are written out with their real costs — treat-as-burned (rotation makes the leaked copy inert; no rewrite; usually right for a signing key) versus rewrite (BFG/filter-repo; rewrites every open PR and invalidates every clone). .gitleaks.toml carries a COMMENTED-OUT allowlist stanza to uncomment AFTER rotation, with an explicit 'DO NOT uncomment before rotation — silencing a live key is worse than the leak, because it also removes the reminder.' EXPECT THE SCHEDULED SCAN TO BE RED until one of those two happens: the key IS still in history, so a finding is the job working, not a broken job. ALSO ADDED: src/test/no-committed-keys.test.ts refuses any tracked .pem/.crx/.p12/.pfx/.keystore/.jks/.key/.ppk at the point a developer notices — their own test run, before the push. It reads git ls-files rather than the filesystem, because an ignored file on disk is fine and a TRACKED one is the bug, and it skips (not fails) without a git binary, since a false red on a P0 guard trains people to ignore it. Negative-verified by force-adding a .pem to the index (reddened naming the file, reverted). REMAINING FOR THE OWNER: (1) rotate the Chrome Web Store signing key and revoke the old one; (2) fill in the storage-location line in key-rotation.md; (3) choose burn-vs-rewrite and, if burning, uncomment the gitleaks stanza. VERIFIED: 3079 tests pass (239 files), tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green, vault-lint 108 notes clean. | SEVERITY RE-ASSESSED 2026-08-03, in BOTH directions, because the original framing is wrong in a way that changes what the owner should do. WORSE THAN RECORDED: the repository is PUBLIC (gh repo view reports visibility PUBLIC) and commit e1dbc4da is on origin, and reading that path out of history still returns a PRIVATE KEY header today. So this is not 'anyone with repo read access' — it is anyone at all, with no access, right now. Untracking the file (AC2) did nothing about that and was never going to; only rotation does. BETTER THAN RECORDED, and this is the part that should stop anyone panicking: the claim that 'anyone can publish an update that every installed user auto-receives' is NOT true today. Checked: no manifest in extension/, extension-condition/ or extension-unified/ declares an update_url or a key field, so there is no self-hosted auto-update channel; and US-1757 (publish to the Chrome Web Store and AMO) is still OPEN and operator-gated, so the extension has never been published and has no installed users. Uploading to the Web Store needs the developer ACCOUNT, which this key is not. WHAT THE KEY ACTUALLY GRANTS: the ability to package a CRX carrying the SAME extension ID as the real one — which matters for sideloading, for enterprise-policy deployment, and for any future self-hosted update channel, and which would let a lookalike be presented as genuine. WHAT THAT MEANS FOR SEQUENCING, which is the practical finding and was recorded nowhere: rotation is CHEAP right now and gets expensive the moment the extension is published, because after publication that ID is the installed identity. So AC1 must be done BEFORE US-1757, and US-1757 should not proceed until it is. RE-VERIFIED the code half rather than trusting the note: git ls-files finds no .pem, .gitignore lines 155-156 refuse *.pem and *.crx (git check-ignore confirms both files), .github/workflows/secret-scan-history.yml exists, and src/test/no-committed-keys.test.ts passes 3/3.
