userStories.title: Impersonation is unbounded, unmarked, non-revocable, and allows account deletion as the user
userStories.description: admin-impersonation.ts:43-132 gets the entry right: super_admin only (:44), users:role scope (:38), fresh step-up (:49), self and privileged targets refused (:54, :68-73), start audited (:116). Everything after the token is minted is open. No time limit — generateLink type magiclink (:90) yields a normal Supabase session for the target, access token plus long-lived refresh token, in the admin's browser, with no cap anywhere. No revocation on stop — src/lib/impersonation.ts:126-129 only redeems the resume token and never calls auth.admin.signOut(targetId), so a copied refresh token outlives the session. No marker — there is no impersonated_by claim and no server-side active-impersonation row, so every request made while impersonating is indistinguishable from the real user's. And destructive actions are fully available: POST /api/account/delete's only server-side control is the confirm string (account.ts:390); the password re-auth at :625-631 is client-side only. A super_admin can impersonate a disputing customer, cancel their subscription and delete their account, and every downstream record shows the customer did it.
acceptanceCriteria: A hard maximum impersonation duration, enforced server-side.
Stopping impersonation revokes the target's sessions.

The impersonated session carries a server-visible marker, and destructive routes (account delete, subscription cancel, marketplace disconnect, grading spend) refuse or require additional authorization while it is set.
The account-delete password re-auth moves server-side.
PRIVILEGED_ROLES (:40) is {admin, super_admin} so a reviewer can be impersonated — decide whether that is intended.
admin-impersonation.ts:137 writes target_id straight from the request body with no check against the start record, so the stop audit row is client-controlled. Fix.
Confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod — it sets the real lifetime of the impersonation and resume tokens.
userStories.notes: [P0][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. A target's own MFA does not protect them: a magiclink redemption yields an aal1 session. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1-AC6 DONE. AC7 is an operator check on prod and stays open. EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED. The entry really is well guarded and the story says so; everything after the token was minted really was open. Confirmed line by line: no cap anywhere, /stop only redeemed the admin's resume token, no marker of any kind, and the stop audit row read target_id straight from the request body. AC1 DONE. NEW admin_impersonation_sessions (00521) plus lib/impersonation-session.ts. Cap is 30 minutes, ENFORCED ON READ rather than by a scheduled sweep — the window between a cap passing and a job noticing is exactly when a forgotten session is most dangerous. And a start that cannot be RECORDED does not happen: a failed insert returns 500 and mints nothing, because a session with no row is precisely the unbounded, unmarked, unrevocable one this story removes. AC2 DONE. /stop revokes the target's sessions through GoTrue's admin logout with scope global. supabase-js cannot do this — auth.admin.signOut wants a JWT, which is the one thing the server does not have — and 'global' is the only scope that reaches a refresh token already copied out of the browser. The result is RETURNED rather than swallowed: an un-revoked stop means the target's tokens are still live and the operator needs to know now. AC3 DONE. The marker is a database row, not a token claim, deliberately: a claim is equally invisible to any route that does not parse it and cannot be revoked once minted. isImpersonated FAILS CLOSED — a lookup error returns true, so a database blip refuses the destructive action. Being wrong that way costs a real user one retry; being wrong the other way is unrecoverable. Guarded by ENUMERATION at eight sites (account delete, buyer + flipdesk subscription cancel, billing portal, and all five marketplace disconnects) rather than by a blanket middleware, which would have to enumerate what is destructive anyway and would silently permit anything it did not know about — the same failure shape US-2354 removed from the scope guard. AC4 DONE. The delete password re-auth moves into the edge, against GoTrue's password grant, and fails CLOSED: an unreachable auth service means the password cannot be proved, and 'cannot prove' must not read as 'proved' on the one endpoint that permanently destroys an account. It deliberately does NOT use the service-role client, which would mint a session — a successful check must prove the password and produce nothing reusable. The browser's local check is REMOVED rather than kept alongside: two places deciding the same thing is how one drifts, and the browser's answer was never the one that mattered. OAuth accounts are exempt on both sides; demanding a password that does not exist is not a control. AC5 DECIDED: reviewer joins PRIVILEGED_ROLES. The set means 'roles whose account carries authority a super_admin should not be able to borrow', not 'roles above a line in the ladder'. A reviewer holds grading:review — they adjust issued grades, which are the product, and RLS grants them human_reviews through is_reviewer_or_admin(). Impersonating one produces a grade adjustment audited to the reviewer rather than to the admin who made it: the same non-repudiation loss the admin exclusion exists to prevent. AC6 DONE: the stop record comes from the START row. The old shape let an admin impersonate one person and log having stopped impersonating another, which is worse than no row because it reads as evidence. A stop with no live session is still audited, with no_active_session set — a double-click and a probe both look like that, and both are worth seeing. PROVEN ON A REAL DATABASE: corpus applied to a throwaway stack, then the target cannot SELECT the row, cannot UPDATE it to end their own impersonation record (0 rows), and the record survives deleting BOTH parties with the emails intact. That last one matters — the record of an impersonation is not the impersonator's to erase. TWO GUARDS CAUGHT MY NEW CODE, both correctly. rls-guard demanded the new table be classified in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY (deny-all in both directions: a readable table leaks operator activity to the person being impersonated, a writable one lets them end the RECORD while the session continues). no-bare-fetch caught both new outbound calls having no deadline — the GoTrue logout runs while an admin waits on /stop, and the password check is the last thing between a request and a permanent deletion. Both go through fetchWithTimeout now. COLUMN NAMING, worth recording: actor_id / target_id rather than actor_user_id / target_user_id, because rls-guard discovers tenant tables by the literal string user_id and this is an operator table that must have no policy at all. Added to the service-role-tables note as a worked example — the existing rule covers ONE owner column and says to call it owner_user_id, which does not help when there are two. A MISTAKE THAT KEEPS RECURRING, so it is written down: my first AC4 assertion searched for the word signInWithPassword and fired on my own comment explaining what the old local check used to do. Second time this session a guard has accused its own prose. It matches a CALL now. NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/impersonation-bounds_test.ts, 10 cases. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS (stop reading the body again, isImpersonated failing open, the guard dropped from one marketplace route), each restored. Vault: NEW vault/20-domain/impersonation.md carries the contract. REMAINING: AC7 — confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod. It sets the real lifetime of the minted impersonation and resume tokens, so it is a SECOND clock running alongside the 30-minute cap: the cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the link stays redeemable. Both should be known. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1317 files, edge suite 5206 passed / 0 failed, web 3225 passed / 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender, vault-lint 135 notes clean. | 2026-08-03 FOLLOW-UP on AC5. The decision landed but its REFUSAL MESSAGE did not: adding reviewer to PRIVILEGED_ROLES left the 403 saying "Impersonating an admin or super-admin is not allowed", so a refused reviewer was told about a rule that was not the one applied. That is not cosmetic — the next operator reads a message that disagrees with the code, concludes the check is broken, and goes hunting a bug that is not there. The message now names all three roles and says WHY (their actions audit to them, not to you), and the new test asserts it against PRIVILEGED_ROLES itself rather than a fixed string, so the two cannot drift apart again. AND THE GUARD WAS SATISFIED BY ITS OWN PROSE — a new variant of the recurring trap. My first version checked the raw source slice, which includes the explanatory comment above the message, and that comment names every role: reverting to the stale message left the case GREEN, passing on prose about the very bug it was written to catch. Only the negative verification found it; the assertion read as correct. It strips comments now. Previous instances of this family accused their own prose; this one was SATISFIED by it, which is the more dangerous direction because nothing fails. AC7 remains and is an OPERATOR/CONFIG check, not a database one: the GoTrue OTP TTL is an env var on the self-hosted auth container (GOTRUE_MAILER_OTP_EXP), so it cannot be added to prod-diagnostics.sql. It matters because it is a SECOND clock — the 30-minute cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the minted link stays redeemable, and the longer of the two is the real exposure. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1338 files, full edge suite 5332 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: The admin scope drift-guard cannot catch an unguarded mutation, and one already shipped
userStories.description: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts:50 computes hasGuard as src.includes('requireScope('), so a single occurrence anywhere in the file satisfies mode 'mutations'. Router mode correctly asserts the use('*') shape (:81-83), but admin-users.ts, admin-bulk.ts, admin-scopes.ts and admin-guarantee-pool.ts are all mutations mode, so a new unguarded .post() in any of them passes CI. This has already happened: admin-bulk.ts:199 POST /resolve has no requireScope at all and adminBulkRoutes has no router-wide guard (:38). It resolves up to 200 arbitrary emails to {id, email, full_name, suspended} — a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle available to any admin regardless of scope.
acceptanceCriteria: The guard parses per-route rather than doing a whole-file substring match.
admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope.
A deliberate no-scope route must be explicitly registered as exempt with a reason, not silently pass.

Note the wider context: the default admin role holds 8 of 9 scopes (rbac-scopes.ts:123-132) and the test actively pins it that way, so scope enforcement is a no-op for a default admin and only becomes a real control once an operator narrows a role. Decide whether that default is right.
userStories.notes: [P1][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-02 EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED, including the one that matters most — the unguarded route really is there. THE GUARD: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts computes const hasGuard = src.includes("requireScope(") — a whole-FILE substring, exactly as reported. For mode "router" it additionally asserts the use("*") shape, so that mode is sound; for mode "mutations" a single requireScope anywhere in the file satisfies it. THE ROUTE THAT ALREADY SLIPPED THROUGH: admin-bulk.ts declares adminBulkRoutes = new Hono<AdminEnv>() with no router-wide use("*"), and its four POSTs are /credits with requireScope("billing:write"), /suspend with requireScope("moderation:write"), /regrade with requireScope("grading:review") — and /resolve with NOTHING. The file passes CI because the other three routes contain the substring. Confirmed what /resolve returns: it accepts up to MAX_TARGETS = 200 entries and answers with {id, email, full_name, suspended} per match, resolved by id OR by email. So it is precisely a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle, available to any admin regardless of scope. AC4's CONTEXT CONFIRMED AND EXACT: SCOPE_KEYS lists nine scopes (billing:write, grading:review, moderation:write, content:publish, users:role, ops:write, marketplace:write, support:write, growth:write) and DEFAULT_ROLE_SCOPES.admin lists eight — every one except users:role. So the story's "8 of 9" is right to the key, and the consequence is worth stating plainly: for a DEFAULT admin, every requireScope call in the codebase except users:role is a no-op. Scope enforcement only becomes a real control after an operator narrows a role, and nothing in the product prompts them to. That makes AC4 the highest-leverage AC here — fixing the guard and adding a scope to /resolve hardens a boundary that, for the default configuration, still admits everyone. IMPLEMENTATION NOTE for AC1: "parse per-route" is more than a regex tweak, because the two shapes are different — a router-wide use("*", requireScope(...)) protects everything after it, while a per-route guard sits as the second argument of .get/.post/.patch/.delete. A parser has to recognise both or it will report false positives on every correctly-guarded router-mode file. The nearest existing model in this repo is the enumeration style used by admin-direct-write-guard.test.ts and items-full-bounded-reads.test.ts: enumerate every route with its guard, and require an explicit DECLARED entry with a reason for any that has none — which is also exactly what AC3 asks for. Note both of those guards were reworked on 2026-08-02 under US-2383 (memoized scan + SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS); copy the fixed shape, not the old one, or the new guard becomes the next flake. | 2026-08-02 AC1 AND AC3 SHIPPED. AC2 DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and the story's framing of it is WRONG — correcting that is the most important part of this note. THE CORRECTION: the story says POST /resolve slipping through is something that "has already happened", implying an accidental omission the weak guard failed to catch. It was not accidental. lib/admin-scope-map.ts's entry for admin-bulk.ts has always carried the rationale "Each bulk op maps to its owning scope: /credits → billing:write, /suspend → moderation:write, /regrade → grading:review. POST /resolve is a read-only target lookup (no scope; US-1562)." So the exemption was a considered, written decision recorded in the very registry the guard reads. The guard's weakness is real and worth fixing; the claim that it let an accident through is not. That distinction matters because AC2 as written ("admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope") is a request to REVERSE a prior decision, not to fix a defect — and doing that silently, from a story that mis-describes how the route got there, is how a considered choice gets undone by someone who never saw the argument. AC1 DONE: "mutations" mode is no longer a whole-file src.includes("requireScope(") check. A new ROUTE_REG parses each mutating registration with a 300-char window (so middleware on a following line still counts) and every one must carry its own requireScope. MEASURED before building it: across all four mutations-mode routers — admin-guarantee-pool, admin-users, admin-scopes, admin-bulk — there are 10 mutating routes and exactly ONE without a scope, POST /resolve. So the change reddens nothing except the known case, which is why it could land as an enforcement rather than a migration. AC3 DONE: NEW ADMIN_ROUTE_SCOPE_EXEMPTIONS in admin-scope-map.ts — file + method + path + a mandatory written reason, enforced at 80 characters so "legacy" cannot be the whole justification. /resolve is registered there with the US-1562 argument stated in full AND the counter-argument from this story stated next to it (the response confirms whether an address has an account, so an admin narrowed to no scopes can still enumerate users; reversing it needs a new read scope, since all three bulk ops would want it). The decision is now data a reviewer can argue with instead of prose inside a rationale string. THE EXEMPTION LIST CANNOT ROT: two further tests make it shrink-only — an entry whose route no longer exists fails, and an entry whose route has SINCE been guarded fails and tells you to delete it, so the allowlist can never be what is permitting a route that the guard would now pass on its own. A third test feeds the parser a known sample (guarded, unguarded, and a multi-line registration) and asserts what it sees, because a regex that silently matches nothing would make the whole guard pass vacuously — the same failure as the substring check, one level down. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, not assumed: a probe route added to admin-users.ts made the guard fail naming POST /__probe_unguarded, and repointing /resolve's exemption at a non-existent path made the staleness test fail with the right message. Both probes reverted, tree confirmed clean. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5042 passed / 0 failed, deno lint clean across 1287 files, deno check clean. AC4 REMAINS OPEN and is still the highest-leverage item: nine scopes exist and the default admin holds eight, so for a default admin every requireScope except users:role is a no-op. Hardening route coverage does not change that; deciding whether the default is right does.

userStories.title: Buyer plan gating: all 13 gate flags are now accounted for — only the free-tier usage count (AC4) is left
userStories.description: lib/buyer-entitlements.ts:221 defines requireBuyerFeature, the 402 upgrade-required guard, and nothing calls it. Its helper buyerFeatureEnabled is used only by it and by tests. So no buyer route enforces plan gating except buyer-authenticity.ts:24, which does its own inline check. buyer-wants.ts — the demand board, a Connoisseur-tier feature — has no gate at all. Every buyer paid feature is available on the free tier.
acceptanceCriteria: Inventory which buyer routes are supposed to be tier-gated, and against which tier.
requireBuyerFeature is applied to each of them.
A test asserts every tier-gated buyer route returns 402 for a free-tier user.
Measure how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather them.
userStories.notes:
[P1][Buyer/Billing] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. The dead-code sweep called this its top finding. Revenue leak, not just dead code. | 2026-08-02 VERIFIED, and quantified. requireBuyerFeature is defined at lib/buyer-entitlements.ts and grep across the whole edge service (excluding _test files) returns ONE hit — its own definition. Zero callers, exactly as reported. buyerFeatureEnabled has two hits: its definition and the single use inside requireBuyerFeature, so the entire gating helper pair is dead. THE SIZE OF THE GAP: BuyerGateFlags in lib/buyer-plans.ts declares THIRTEEN gated features — extensionSecondOpinion, discrepancyScoring, priceFairness, conditionAlerts, fitPrediction, authenticityAddon, videoGrading, rewards, trustScore, purchaseGuarantee, wardrobePortfolio, demandBoard, prioritySupport. Across the seven buyer route files, exactly ONE reads a gate flag: buyer-authenticity.ts checks ent.gateFlags.authenticityAddon inline. buyer-closet.ts, buyer-purchases.ts, buyer-rewards.ts, buyer-trust.ts and buyer-wants.ts contain no gate reference at all (buyer-profile.ts's only hit is the word "entitlements" in a comment). So one of thirteen flags is enforced anywhere, and the story's specific example holds — buyer-wants.ts, the demand board, has no gate. A DETAIL THAT CHANGES AC2 AND IS NOT IN THE STORY: the one gate that does exist returns 403 with code "not_entitled", while requireBuyerFeature is the 402 upgrade-required guard. They are not interchangeable. Applying requireBuyerFeature to buyer-authenticity as part of AC2 would change its status code from 403 to 402, which is a client-visible change — the buyer web/iOS clients may branch on one or the other. Either check the clients first, or leave authenticity on 403 and say why. Do not assume the helper is a drop-in for the inline check just because both deny. SEQUENCING NOTE on AC4: it asks how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather. That is a PROD query this host cannot run, and it should gate AC2 rather than follow it — switching thirteen features on at once for users who have had them free is a support event, not just a fix. Split AC4 out as an operator task so AC1 (the inventory) can proceed without it. AC1 is the cheap half and is mostly done by this note: the thirteen flags above are the candidate list, and what remains is deciding the TIER each belongs to, which is a product call rather than a code reading. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1, AC2 and AC3 DONE. AC4 is a prod query this host cannot run and stays open as the operator half. AC1, the inventory, is now a FILE rather than a paragraph: services/edge-functions/src/tests/buyer-plan-gates_test.ts lists all 21 buyer routes across the seven route files, each with either the feature that gates it or a stated reason it is open. AC2: TWO ROUTES WERE GENUINELY UNPROTECTED and are now gated. The demand board (POST /wants, PATCH /wants/:id) is Connoisseur-only and had no gate on any of its four routes. The purchase-guarantee claim (POST /purchases/:id/claim) is Guard and up and had none either. Both now call requireBuyerFeature and RETURN its refusal. The claim gate goes BEFORE the ownership read on purpose: a free-tier buyer should be told to upgrade, not told whether some other buyer's purchase id exists. A RULE I HAD TO INVENT, because the story does not state one and the naive reading causes harm: GATE THE PATHS THAT CREATE OR CONSUME A PAID FEATURE, NEVER THE ONES THAT READ OR REMOVE WHAT THE BUYER ALREADY HAS. Gating GET /wants and DELETE /wants/:id would mean a buyer who downgrades cannot see or clean up wants they created while paying — the gate would convert a billing state into data loss. Both are left open with that reason recorded at the call site and in the registry. WHAT I DID NOT GATE, and why each: eleven routes read a flag that is TRUE ON EVERY TIER (wardrobePortfolio, extensionSecondOpinion, rewards, trustScore), so a gate there denies nobody and costs a database round trip — a test case now FAILS if anyone claims a gate on a feature no tier withholds, because a gate that cannot deny reads as protection and is not. POST /authenticity keeps its inline 403 not_entitled rather than being converted: requireBuyerFeature returns 402, and the buyer web and iOS clients may branch on the status. That is a client contract change and belongs in its own story rather than in a sweep — the previous pass flagged this and it was right. AC3: the story asks for a live 402 assertion for a free-tier user. That needs an authenticated request against a seeded buyer, i.e. the database, so I did NOT claim it and built the strongest thing that works without one — six cases asserting the guard is CALLED on the right route with the right feature name, that its refusal is RETURNED rather than discarded, that the declared route set IS the route set, that every ungated route carries a real reason, and that the free tier genuinely lacks demandBoard and purchaseGuarantee (otherwise the two new gates would silently stop denying anyone while every other case still passed). WHY ENUMERATION: dead security code is the worst kind, because the helper's EXISTENCE is what makes a reviewer believe the gating is handled. Nothing about reading buyer-wants.ts said "this is ungated" — the absence was the bug, and absence is what a diff never shows. A new buyer route now fails until its author answers the question nobody asked for thirteen features. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FOUR WAYS: removed the demand-board gate (reddened naming the route and flag), kept the call but discarded its Response (reddened on the return), added an undeclared /probe route (reddened as an unlisted route), and re-declared the claim gate against the rewards flag (reddened as a gate that denies nobody). Each restored. A MISTAKE WORTH RECORDING: my first route regex was a bare .get( / .post(, which also matched c.get("userId") in every handler and reported a phantom route per file. Over-matching is not harmless here — it would have left the guard permanently red, and a permanently red guard gets deleted. It is anchored to the Routes receiver now and says so. AND A SELF-INFLICTED ONE: I reverted my own uncommitted gate edits with a git checkout while restoring a negative-verification probe, then caught it by grepping for the guard before moving on. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1310 files, full edge suite 5166 passed / 0 failed, tenant-isolation 17/0. REMAINING: AC4 (how many free-tier buyers have been using the demand board and the guarantee claim, to decide grandfathering) is a prod query — it belongs with the other operator diagnostics in scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql. Worth doing BEFORE this deploys, since switching a feature off for users who have had it free is a support event, not just a fix. | 2026-08-03: this story's last open AC is now answerable by scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql, which the operator runs in ONE psql session alongside the other blocked stories. Read-only, verified by executing against a real database with ON_ERROR_STOP=1 — so it cannot fail the operator's session on a wrong column name, which is the failure mode that makes someone distrust the whole file. §12 counts free-tier accounts that used the two features that were genuinely ungated — the demand board and the guarantee claim — BY ACCOUNT rather than by row, because '3,000 wants' and '4 buyers' call for very different decisions about grandfathering. A 30-day slice is reported separately: an account that used it once a year ago is not the same support problem as one using it this week. | AC4 FIRST DATA POINT, 2026-08-03 (owner ran the diagnostics): free_tier_accounts_last_30d = 0. No free-tier buyer has used the demand board in the last 30 days, so switching its gate on is NOT a support event for anyone currently active. That is the half of AC4 that decides urgency. What is still needed to close it is the ALL-TIME half from the same section — the demand_board and guarantee_claim rows of the first query in §12 — because an account that used the feature months ago still loses access on the next deploy, and whether that matters is a grandfathering call rather than a code one. | PROD ANSWER 2026-08-03 (owner ran scripts/prod-diagnostics-console.sql). §12's 30-day slice returned 0. Combined with the earlier reading, no free-tier buyer has used the demand board recently. STILL MISSING: the ALL-TIME half of §12 — the demand_board and guarantee_claim rows of that section's first query — which is what decides grandfathering for someone who used the feature months ago and would lose it on the next deploy. | 2026-08-04 RE-CHECKED — the title is now FALSE and should not be quoted. grep for requireBuyerFeature across services/edge-functions/src excluding tests returns four hits: its definition in lib/buyer-entitlements.ts plus three real call sites — buyer-purchases.ts:301 gating purchaseGuarantee, and buyer-wants.ts:40 and :91 gating demandBoard. Commit 6e3915f7 closed the zero-caller claim, and the story's own worked example (the demand board) is one of the routes now gated. WHAT REMAINS is the count, not the mechanism: the earlier note recorded THIRTEEN flags in BuyerGateFlags, and two of them are now enforced through this helper (a third, authenticityAddon, is enforced inline in buyer-authenticity.ts). So AC1 (the inventory of which routes gate against which tier) and AC2 (applying it to each) are still open for the remaining ten, and AC4 (measuring free-tier usage before deciding whether to grandfather) is untouched. Keep the story, retitle it to something like 'Ten of thirteen buyer gate flags are still unenforced' — the current title will read as stale to the next person and invites closing it by mistake.

| 2026-08-08 RETITLED, as the previous note asked, and the number in the old title was wrong in BOTH directions.

The 2026-08-04 note said to retitle this to "Ten of thirteen buyer gate flags are still unenforced". I checked that number instead of adopting it, and it does not survive. THE REAL ACCOUNTING, measured by grepping every flag name across the whole edge service:

FIVE FLAGS ARE TRUE ON EVERY TIER — extensionSecondOpinion, conditionAlerts, rewards, trustScore, wardrobePortfolio. Nothing withholds them from anyone, so there is no revenue to leak and a gate on them would be decoration plus a database round trip. They were being counted as unenforced. They are not enforceable.

THE OTHER EIGHT ARE DENIABLE, AND ALL EIGHT ARE ENFORCED — just not all in the buyer route files, which is the whole reason the count kept reading wrong. A route-shaped audit of seven buyer files cannot see five of them:
  demandBoard, purchaseGuarantee -> requireBuyerFeature 402 (buyer-wants.ts x2, buyer-purchases.ts)
  authenticityAddon -> inline 403 not_entitled (buyer-authenticity.ts), deliberately not converted
  discrepancyScoring, priceFairness, fitPrediction -> FIELD SUPPRESSION via resolveExtensionGates in routes/public-grading.ts:1107-1122 and :1818 — the extension scan returns, with the paid fields nulled
  videoGrading -> 402 UPGRADE_REQUIRED at routes/grade.ts:617, after the seller plan is checked and the buyer plan is the second way in
  prioritySupport -> NO runtime path by design; lib/plan-gate.ts:52 states it is an SLA/routing attribute

THE SHAPES DIFFER AND ALL OF THEM ARE RIGHT. A 402 on the extension scan would refuse the free feature in order to withhold the paid one; suppressing three fields is the correct answer there. Writing a test that demanded one uniform shape would have pushed three of these toward the wrong one — worth saying, because that is the obvious next move and it would be a regression.

NEW GUARD, the flag side of the question this story was actually filed on: buyer-plan-gates_test.ts already enumerated all 21 ROUTES, which answers "is this route gated?" and cannot answer "is this paid feature enforced anywhere?". FLAG_ENFORCEMENT now maps every BuyerGateFlags key to null / "GATES" / a file path. A null entry must be true on every tier (so "we do not gate it" stays earned, not assumed); a "GATES" entry must appear in the route registry; a file entry is READ and must still mention the flag, so deleting an enforcement reddens here instead of leaving the table describing code that used to exist. The Record type forces exhaustiveness one way; a key-set assertion catches the other.

NEGATIVE-VERIFIED TWICE: flipped rewards to false on the free tier (reddened, naming rewards and free — a paid feature nothing withholds); repointed videoGrading at lib/plan-gate.ts (reddened, naming the file that no longer mentions it). Both restored, 7 passed. deno lint + deno check clean.

STILL passes:false ON AC4 ALONE, unchanged: the ALL-TIME half of scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql section 12 — how many free-tier accounts EVER used the demand board or the guarantee claim, which decides grandfathering. The 30-day slice already came back 0 twice. Operator query; this host cannot run it.

userStories.title: Variation listings cannot be revised: resubmit needs an offer id a group listing never has
userStories.description: As a seller with a multi-variation eBay listing, I want Save and resubmit to push my edits to eBay, so that a listing with size or color variants is not frozen the moment it goes live.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /api/flipdesk/ebay/listings/:id/revise on a listing whose listings.variations is non-null and whose platform_offer_id is null no longer returns the 409 "This listing has no eBay offer id" (flipdesk-ebay.ts, the guard above the offerId const) and instead revises through the eBay inventory item group.

The revise resolves its strategy group-FIRST, the same way the end path does via resolveEndStrategy (flipdesk-ebay.ts:8836), and keys the group on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku rather than the current inventory_items.sku, so a SKU rename cannot orphan the live group.

The group branch updates every variant inventory item and then calls createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup (both already exported from services/edge-functions/src/lib/ebay-client.ts), so title, description, price, photos and specifics changes reach the live listing.

A single-offer listing keeps the existing offer branch byte-for-byte; a deno test in services/edge-functions/src/tests/listing-variations_test.ts asserts both branches are chosen correctly from a listings row (variations present versus platform_offer_id present).

The composer treats a published variation listing as live: isLiveListing in src/pages/flipdesk/composer.tsx stops requiring platform_offer_id when listings.variations is present and platform_listing_id is set, so the footer shows Save and resubmit to eBay instead of offering to publish an already-live listing. A vitest guard pins that gate.

Tenant scoping is unchanged: the revise route still reaches the listing through an owner-verified parent row (US-268), and services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts gains a case covering the group-revise branch.

Verified after deploy against a real multi-variation listing, not by reading code: the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group (the variation listingPayload in flipdesk-ebay.ts omits it), so unit tests alone cannot prove the round trip.
userStories.notes: PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC2, AC4 and AC5 DONE, plus a truthful refusal in place of misleading advice. AC1, AC3, AC6 and AC7 remain, and the reason is scoped rather than vague. VERIFIED THE WHOLE CHAIN FIRST. The revise route really does begin with `if (!row.listing.platform_offer_id) return 409`, eBay really never mints an offer id for a listing published through publish_by_inventory_item_group, and loadListingOwned already selects both `variations` and the pinned `inventory_sku`. The END path already solved the same problem correctly under US-1999 (resolveEndStrategy, group-first, keyed on the pinned SKU) — two resolvers in one file giving different answers to the same question is the shape that made this findable. AC2 DONE: NEW resolveReviseStrategy, deliberately the same shape and the same ORDER as resolveEndStrategy. Group first, because an offer-first resolver reads a group listing as having no mechanism at all — which is precisely the bug. Keyed on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku, since the inventory_item_group was created under the base SKU at publish and a later rename would aim the revise at a group that does not exist. One deliberate difference from the end resolver: no-mechanism is `none`, not `local`. Ending locally is a real outcome — the listing is closed in FlipDesk — whereas a revise with no mechanism has done nothing and must not report otherwise. A test pins both the agreement and that single divergence. AC5 DONE, AND IT WAS THE WORSE HALF OF THE BUG. isLiveListing required a platform_offer_id, so every LIVE variation listing was classified as a DRAFT and the footer offered to "Publish to eBay" something already live. The 409 at least refused; this invited the seller to publish a duplicate of their own listing. The gate now also accepts variations + platform_listing_id — the eBay item id publish-by-group returns — and a test requires BOTH halves, since a matrix alone would call an unpublished draft live. SHIPPED AHEAD OF THE FEATURE, on purpose: the 409 for a variation listing no longer says "Sync from eBay or republish to enable edits". That is advice that CANNOT WORK — republishing does not create an offer id for a group, and republishing a live listing is worse than doing nothing. It now says the truth: group revise is not supported yet, edit on eBay for now. A wrong instruction is worse than a plain refusal, and this one was pointing sellers at an action that could duplicate their listing. AC4 DONE: seven cases appended to listing-variations_test.ts covering both branches from a listings row, the ordering (group wins even when a stale offer id is present), the pinned-SKU key, the two no-mechanism shapes, the revise/end agreement, and the refusal text. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED: the resolver flipped to offer-first (reddened on the ordering case) and the composer's variation branch reduced to the matrix alone (reddened on the both-halves case). WHAT REMAINS AND WHY I DID NOT DO IT. AC1/AC3 are the group-revise branch itself: update every variant inventory item, then createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup. The machinery exists — publishVariationListing does exactly this — but reusing it means reconstructing a PublishContextOk, PublishItem, policies and photos inside the revise handler, and that function also performs publish-shaped PERSISTENCE which a revise must not repeat. It is a substantial change to the most sensitive file in the service, on the path every seller's Save-and-resubmit uses, and AC7 states plainly that unit tests cannot prove the round trip because the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group. Half-implementing it risks breaking the COMMON single-offer revise to fix the rare one. The resolver, the composer gate and the honest refusal are the parts that are safe and testable now; the branch wants one deliberate pass with a real multi-variation listing to verify against, which is what AC7 asks for anyway. AC6 (the tenant-isolation case) belongs with that branch — there is no new query to scope yet. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1323 files, edge suite 5245 passed / 0 failed, web 260 files / 3236 tests 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender. | 2026-08-09 AC1/AC3 SCOPED, NOT IMPLEMENTED, and there is a SEMANTIC DECISION nobody has taken that the ACs do not mention. Recorded so the next session finds it before writing the branch rather than after. AC3 reads as plumbing: update every variant inventory item, then call createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup, both already exported. Traced the publish path (flipdesk-ebay.ts:7650-7740) to mirror it, and the plumbing IS that shape. THE PROBLEM IS WHAT A SCALAR EDIT MEANS TO A MATRIX. The revise route accepts title, description, listing_price, quantity and photos. For a variation listing those split cleanly in two: TITLE, DESCRIPTION and PHOTOS are unambiguous — they live on the group AND on every member item, so a revise applies them to both, exactly as publish does. PRICE and QUANTITY are NOT. The publish path creates ONE OFFER PER VARIANT SKU, each with its own price (the per-variant override, else the base) and its own quantity (variant.quantity). A single listing_price in the revise body has no defined meaning against that: does it overwrite every variant's price, or only the ones with no override, or set a new base the overrides continue to shift from? Each answer is defensible and they produce different money on a LIVE listing. Same for quantity against variant.quantity. Guessing here is not a call code should make — it is the same class of decision as the offer-route-vs-return-route split in US-2227, and the wrong guess silently reprices a seller's whole variation matrix. RECOMMENDED SHAPE, if the decision goes the obvious way: implement the group branch for title/description/photos only, and REFUSE price/quantity on a variation listing with a message naming eBay as the place to change them — the same truthful-refusal pattern this story already used in place of the misleading 'republish to enable edits' advice. That ships the majority of the value with no ambiguity, and leaves the pricing question to be decided on its own rather than smuggled in. WHY I DID NOT IMPLEMENT IT THIS PASS, stated plainly rather than dressed up: this is a mutation path against live eBay listings, AC7 already says it cannot be verified without a real multi-variation listing, and I have no way to exercise it end to end from here. A branch that looks right and is wrong is worse than the current honest 409, because the 409 loses an edit and a bad branch loses a listing's pricing. The unambiguous half is genuinely small once the price/quantity decision is recorded; it is the decision that gates it, not the code. AC6 IS COUPLED, NOT INDEPENDENT: tenant-isolation_test.ts already covers 'B cannot revise A's eBay listing' via loadListingOwned (line ~1930), and a VARIATION-specific case needs a seeded variation listing id the fixture does not have (seed-tenant-isolation-fixture.ts) plus a group branch to actually exercise. Adding it before the branch exists would assert the refusal, not the ownership check. VERIFIED UNCHANGED: resolveReviseStrategy (AC2), the composer's isLiveListing fix (AC5) and the truthful 409 all still in place; full edge suite green this session at 6213 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: A denied function call from anon or authenticated SEGFAULTS Postgres and restarts the whole database
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want a permission-denied RPC to return an error instead of crashing the database, so that anyone holding the public anon key cannot restart production at will.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish whether the PROD Postgres image reproduces it. On the local Supabase image (PG 17.6) it reproduces every time; prod is a separate self-hosted image and this has NOT been tested there, deliberately, because the test is a denial of service against production. The safe check is to read the image tag and the supautils.hint_roles setting, not to call a denied RPC.

If prod reproduces: mitigate BEFORE anything else. Clearing supautils.hint_roles (it exists only to append a GRANT hint to the error message) or upgrading the image are the two candidates; whichever is chosen, prove it with a denied call against a staging copy of the same image.

A regression check that survives an image upgrade: a throwaway-stack test that revokes EXECUTE on a scratch function, calls it as anon, and asserts a clean 'permission denied for function' error with the connection still alive.

supabase/migrations/00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED is renamed back to .sql, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped to 00527 in the same commit, and US-2282 closed — the SQL is already written and verified, it is only blocked on this.

The 5 functions already revoked from anon before this was known (refund_grade 00048, credit_ledger_reconciliation 00093, release_job_lock + try_acquire_job_lock 00094, reserve_snap/refund_snap 00099, reconcile_payout_link 00117, equity_snapshot_owners) are enumerated in the notes as the CURRENTLY reachable crash entry points, since they are what an attacker could use today.
userStories.notes: [P0][Security/DB] Found 2026-08-04 by accident while verifying US-2282 on a throwaway stack, and it is the reason US-2282 is not shipping. ISOLATED, not guessed — four probes on the local Supabase image (PostgreSQL 17.6, shared_preload_libraries includes supautils): (1) a trivial scratch function with EXECUTE revoked, called as anon => SIGNAL 11 SEGMENTATION FAULT, 'terminating any other active server processes', full database recovery; (2) same as authenticated => same crash; (3) same as a custom role NOT listed in supautils.hint_roles => clean 'ERROR: permission denied for function', connection alive; (4) a denied TABLE read as anon => clean error PLUS the supautils hint 'Grant the required privileges to the current role with: GRANT SELECT ON public.applied_migrations TO anon;'. supautils.hint_roles is set to exactly 'anon, authenticated, service_role', which is exactly the set that crashes. So the crash is in the supautils hint path for FUNCTION permission denials specifically; the table path is fine. ALREADY REACHABLE TODAY, WITHOUT ANY NEW MIGRATION: public.refund_grade(uuid) has been revoked from anon since 00048/00093, and calling it as anon crashes the database the same way — verified, not inferred. PostgREST exposes it as an RPC, so the input needed is the public anon key and one HTTP call. WHY US-2282 IS BLOCKED ON THIS RATHER THAN THE OTHER WAY AROUND: 00527 does not create the bug, it multiplies the entry points — from the handful of functions already revoked to ~80. Applying it into an unpatched image would hand an attacker eighty ways to restart the database instead of eight. The SQL is written, verified on a fresh stack, and parked at supabase/migrations/00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED; the .BLOCKED suffix is what keeps apply-prod-migrations.sh (which globs *.sql) from applying it. NOT TESTED AGAINST PROD ON PURPOSE. The test IS the denial of service, so running it would be the attack. The safe next step is to read the prod image tag and 'show supautils.hint_roles' over psql — both read-only — and compare against the local image. If prod's image differs enough not to reproduce, this closes as a local-only artifact and US-2282 unblocks immediately. | 2026-08-08 AC3 DONE; AC5 DONE AND THE COUNT WAS WRONG; AC1/AC2 now have a PROVEN mitigation and a safer prod probe. Docker was available on this host for the first time, so every claim below was re-run rather than inherited. REPRODUCED on public.ecr.aws/supabase/postgres:17.6.1.106 with all 552 migrations applied: a scratch function with EXECUTE revoked, called as anon, gives 'server closed the connection' and the server log shows 'terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault' -> 'terminating any other active server processes' -> 'automatic recovery in progress'. ALSO reproduced with public.refund_grade(uuid), a REAL function that has been revoked from anon since 00048/00093 — so this is reachable in prod today with the public anon key and one RPC call, exactly as the story claimed. MITIGATION PROVEN (this is new): setting supautils.hint_roles = '' in /etc/postgresql-custom/supautils.conf and restarting Postgres turns the same call into a clean 'ERROR: permission denied for function' with the connection alive. Verified by flipping the config both ways twice. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT FOR WHOEVER APPLIES IT: this CANNOT be done from SQL or from a migration — supautils rejects 'ALTER SYSTEM SET supautils.hint_roles' with 'permission denied to set parameter' even as the postgres superuser. It is a postgresql.conf change on the host (Coolify), i.e. an operator action, and no migration in this repo can substitute for it. AC5 CORRECTED: the story listed ~8 reachable entry points; the real number is 14, enumerated from the live schema rather than by hand (select ... where not has_function_privilege('anon', oid, 'EXECUTE') over the 160 public functions): admin_adjust_credits, bump_cache_signal, credit_ledger_reconciliation, delete_account, get_cache_signal, latest_schema_migration, reconcile_payout_link, record_registered_number_sighting, record_style_code_observation, refund_grade, release_job_lock, reserve_guarantee_pool_drawdown, revoke_grade_credits, try_acquire_job_lock. AC3 SHIPPED: scripts/db-denied-rpc-crash-check.mjs, wired into verify.mjs --db and db-migrations.yml. It is ADVISORY (continue-on-error), NOT a gate, and that is a deliberate call recorded in both files: the stock image is vulnerable today, so gating would turn every migration PR red on arrival, and this repo already has the lesson that a permanently red guard gets switched off (US-1927 notes). Flipping it to a hard gate is step ONE of the mitigation, not a follow-up. VERIFIED BOTH DIRECTIONS with the final code: RED on the stock image (all three assertions fire), GREEN with hint_roles cleared. Three self-inflicted defects were found and fixed while building it, all the same class as bugs this repo has shipped before — an assertion on pg_postmaster_start_time() that CANNOT EVER FIRE (a backend SIGSEGV is handled by crash recovery; the postmaster never restarts), and twice using execFileSync where the text being asserted on is on STDERR (both the 'permission denied' string and the Postgres server log), which silently compared against an empty string. AC1 — A SAFE PROBE THAT WAS MISSED, worth trying before anything invasive: US-1927's 2026-07-18 note records that calling latest_schema_migration() against PROD as anon returned 42501 permission denied rather than a crash. latest_schema_migration is on the list of 14 above, so IF that observation was a real prod call it is evidence prod does NOT reproduce — and it cost nothing. Treat it as a lead, not proof: it is second-hand, and it is not certain the 42501 came from Postgres rather than from PostgREST's own check. Re-running that one read-only call is the cheapest next step and is not an attack. EVIDENCE POINTING THE OTHER WAY: vault/10-ops/backups.md:161 records the 2026-06-12 restore drill against 'the same Supabase image as prod' pinned at 17.6.1.106 — the exact image that crashes here. Nothing in the repo pins the prod tag, so that drill log is the only signal, and it suggests prod DOES reproduce. These two point opposite ways; resolve with the read-only check the story already specifies (read the image tag and 'show supautils.hint_roles' over psql). KEPT passes:false: AC1 (prod image determination) and AC2 (apply the mitigation) are operator actions on the Coolify host that cannot be done or validated from here, and AC4 (unblock 00527 / US-2282) must stay blocked until AC2 is done — applying it into an unpatched image would take the entry points from 14 to ~80.

userStories.title: Prod Postgres + storage host has no full-disk encryption — a pulled or reclaimed VPS disk is readable plaintext
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want the block device holding prod Postgres and the Supabase storage volume to be encrypted at rest, so that a decommissioned, snapshotted or physically seized Contabo disk does not hand over every grade, user address, credit ledger row and garment photo in plaintext.
acceptanceCriteria: The prod host's Postgres data directory and the Supabase storage volume (STORAGE_DIR=/var/lib/supabase/storage, per vault/10-ops/backups.md:75) both sit on a LUKS-encrypted block device — verified by 'lsblk -o NAME,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINT' showing crypto_LUKS under the mountpoint, not by reading a runbook.

The LUKS passphrase/keyfile is stored in the same secrets manager as the other prod secrets and is listed in vault/10-ops/key-rotation.md's rotation table with its rotation procedure, alongside EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

A documented unlock path exists for unattended reboot (keyfile on a separate volume, or clevis/tang, or an explicit 'operator must unlock manually' decision) and vault/10-ops/incident-response.md records what happens to uptime if the host reboots while nobody is available to unlock.
vault/10-ops/deploy.md gains a section stating the encryption status of the prod volumes, so a future operator rebuilding the host does not silently recreate it unencrypted.

SECURITY.md's at-rest paragraph (currently line 44, which claims only 'Marketplace OAuth tokens are encrypted at rest') is updated to state the volume-level posture accurately — either encrypted, or explicitly not.

userStories.title: Offsite backups are uploaded unencrypted — R2 credentials alone yield a full plaintext database dump
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want every backup artifact encrypted with a key we hold before it leaves the host, so that compromise of the Cloudflare R2 bucket or its rclone credentials does not expose the entire production database and every uploaded garment photo.
acceptanceCriteria: scripts/ops/backup-postgres.sh encrypts the pg_dump artifact with a key held by GradeThread (age or gpg) BEFORE the 'rclone copy' at line 55, so the object landing in r2:gradethread-backups/pg is ciphertext. R2's own server-side encryption does not satisfy this AC — the threat model is a leaked R2 credential, which server-side encryption is transparent to.

The .sha256 sidecar (backup-postgres.sh:50) is computed over the ENCRYPTED artifact, so the existing 'dump plus its .sha256 in the last 24h' offsite check from vault/10-ops/backups.md:50 still verifies what is actually stored.

scripts/ops/backup-storage.sh either encrypts the storage mirror or the runbook explicitly records the decision not to, with the reason — an rclone sync of the raw storage volume today exposes every submission image, including grading label photos, to anyone with the R2 credential.

scripts/ops/restore-postgres.sh and restore-drill.sh decrypt before pg_restore, and a restore drill against an ENCRYPTED artifact passes and is recorded in the drill table at vault/10-ops/backups.md:162 — an encryption change that breaks restore is worse than no encryption.

The backup encryption key is added to vault/10-ops/key-rotation.md's rotation table with a stated procedure, and the procedure covers the window where old ciphertext in the 30-day-retention bucket was written under the previous key.
vault/10-ops/backups.md documents that losing the backup key means losing every backup, and names where the key is stored (a reference, never the value).
userStories.notes: 2026-08-08 ALL SIX ACs BUILT AND VERIFIED END TO END; kept passes:false because the mechanism is done and PRODUCTION HAS NOT MOVED — the keypair does not exist yet and the updated scripts are not on the DB host. Docker plus an age implementation were both available here, so nothing below is reasoned-about; every claim was run. MECHANISM (AC1): backup-postgres.sh encrypts the dump with age to BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT before rclone copy. PUBLIC-key on purpose — the DB host holds only the recipient half, so it can encrypt but not decrypt, and rooting the database box does not also hand over the offsite archive. It FAILS CLOSED: with RCLONE_REMOTE set and no recipient it exits 1 having called rclone ZERO times (verified with a stub rclone on PATH that logs its argv). Happy path verified the same way: the only two objects handed to rclone are .dump.age and .dump.age.sha256, never the plaintext .dump. AC2: the sha256 is computed over the CIPHERTEXT, which is what the bucket actually holds. FOUND AND FIXED A PRE-EXISTING BUG WHILE DOING IT, and it would have bitten during a real recovery: sha256sum \"\" wrote the sidecar with the ABSOLUTE staging path (/backups/pg/...), and restore-postgres.sh verifies with sha256sum -c, which resolves whatever path the sidecar records. On a scratch host that path does not exist, so verification failed with 'No such file or directory' — i.e. the checksum could never have passed on any genuine offsite restore, only on the machine that wrote it. Both branches now cd first and record a BARE FILENAME. Proved by backing up to one directory, copying the artifact to another (what an offsite fetch does), and restoring successfully from there. AC3 (storage): the age-per-file approach does NOT fit an incremental rclone sync of thousands of objects — pre-encrypting per run breaks rclone's diffing. The mechanism is rclone's own CRYPT REMOTE (client-side, per object, sync still works), which is config-side, so what the script can enforce is refusal: backup-storage.sh reads 'rclone config show <remote>' and exits unless type = crypt, overridable only by an explicit STORAGE_BACKUP_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT=1. Checked against the config rather than the remote's NAME, because a remote called 'r2crypt' that is not of type crypt would otherwise read as safe. AC4 (the one the story warns about most — 'an encryption change that breaks restore is worse than no encryption'): restore-postgres.sh detects a .age input, verifies the checksum BEFORE decrypting (checking the stored object, not a derived one), decrypts to a mktemp file chmod 600 created empty before any plaintext is written, and shreds it via an EXIT trap — verified 0 leftover temp files after a run. restore-drill.sh now performs the encrypt/sha/verify/decrypt round-trip on EVERY run under an EPHEMERAL keypair, so the drill never touches the real key and a drill can no longer silently measure a procedure prod does not use (opt out only via DRILL_SKIP_ENCRYPTION=1). Drill PASS recorded in vault/10-ops/backups.md: migration 00559, 5 users, 20 submissions, 375 RLS policies all matched, dump 1s restore 5s. NOTE ON DRILL QUALITY: the first run passed with every row count at ZERO, which makes each 'OK' vacuous — a data-restore failure would have passed too. Seeded real rows and re-ran; the recorded numbers are from that run. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, all four directions: no recipient => refuses and uploads nothing; no identity => refuses to restore; a single flipped byte in the ciphertext => checksum FAILS before decryption is attempted; and the drill asserts the .age artifact is NOT still a readable pg_dump (a passthrough bug would otherwise leave everything green while backups shipped in the clear). DOCS (AC5, AC6): key-rotation.md gains both keys in the rotation table plus a full section — the asymmetry that makes this key unlike every other one is that losing it is SILENT (backups keep running, /health stays green, the bucket keeps filling; you find out at the only moment it matters), and the 30-day-retention window means deleting the old identity on rotation day destroys most of the recovery range, so both identities are kept until the lifecycle rule has aged out the last object under the old one. backups.md gains an Encryption section saying plainly that losing the key loses every backup with no escrow and no support path, requiring two independent durable homes neither of which is the machine being backed up, and naming Infisical as the home for the identity (a reference, never a value) while noting it is NOT an app env var and no deployment surface reads it. Also corrected the offsite-freshness check there: the objects to look for are now .dump.age / .dump.age.sha256, and a bare .dump in the bucket means an OLD script is still deployed and the nightly is shipping plaintext. encryption-at-rest.md is the security-questionnaire page and carries these scripts in its code_refs, so it was updated in the same change per the vault same-commit rule — its store table and gap paragraph now say 'mechanism yes, production not yet' and explicitly tell the reader NOT to upgrade the customer-facing answer until the key exists on the host. vault:lint --strict green, all four ops scripts pass bash -n. REMAINING (operator, on the Contabo/Coolify DB host — this is the whole gap): (1) age-keygen the pair, put the identity in Infisical plus one offline copy, put the public recipient in /etc/cron.d/gradethread-backups; (2) rclone config a crypt remote and repoint the storage cron at it; (3) deploy the updated scripts to /opt/gradethread. Step-by-step is in the MANUAL callout in vault/10-ops/backups.md. Until all three are done prod backups remain plaintext, which is why this stays open. WORTH KNOWING: age has no Windows package, but rage (the Rust build, format-compatible) does — 'scoop install rage', then AGE_BIN=rage. Every script takes AGE_BIN, which is how the drill ran on this host.

userStories.title: Postal addresses and phone numbers are stored as plaintext columns while OAuth tokens next to them are AES-GCM encrypted
userStories.description: As a reseller, I want my home or business street address stored encrypted the same way my marketplace tokens are, so that a single leaked database dump or a SQL-injection read does not hand an attacker a mailing list of resellers with valuable inventory at those addresses.
acceptanceCriteria: public.users.ship_from_address (jsonb, added by 00325_user_business_shipping_profile.sql) and public.users.business_phone are stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext produced by services/edge-functions/src/lib/crypto-aes.ts encryptToken(), with the owning user id passed as the aad option so a ciphertext copied onto another user's row fails to decrypt (US-268 tenant binding, same pattern as the marketplace token columns).

public.measure_card_requests street fields (ship_name, address_line1, address_line2, city, postal_code — added by 00351_measure_card_requests.sql) are encrypted the same way, keyed to owner_user_id. state and country stay plaintext so the fulfillment export can still filter and sort by region without decrypting every row.

A migration ships the US-1108 triple: idempotent SQL (safe to re-run on any prior state), EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in services/edge-functions/src/lib/schema-version.ts in the SAME commit, and the self-record footer inserting its version into public.applied_migrations.

The migration backfills existing plaintext rows to ciphertext, and the read path tolerates both during the rollout — a row that does not parse as v1:/v2: is returned as-is rather than throwing, so a partial backfill cannot 500 the Settings page.

Every edge route that reads or writes these columns decrypts/encrypts at the boundary and stays tenant-scoped per US-268, with a case added to services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts.

The eBay ship-from location prefill (US-1442's original consumer) still populates correctly end to end after the change — verified against the flipdesk-ebay.ts path that consumes ship_from_address, not just by unit test.
A test asserts that decrypting a ship_from_address ciphertext with a DIFFERENT user id as aad throws, proving the tenant binding is real.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-08 AC2 DONE, AC4 and AC7 DONE for it, and AC1 IS BLOCKED ON A PREREQUISITE THE STORY DOES NOT NAME. The prerequisite is the most important thing in this note, because AC1 reads like a one-file change and is not. AC1 IS NOT REACHABLE YET, and it is a fact about the write path rather than a preference. src/pages/settings.tsx:306 writes users.business_phone and users.ship_from_address DIRECTLY from the browser with supabase-js under RLS, and 00526_users_self_update_allowlist.sql (restated in 00550) explicitly allowlists both columns. They are READ the same way in three places: settings.tsx:141-143, flipdesk/marketplaces.tsx:202 and lib/account-export.ts:54. EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is an edge-only secret and must stay one, so encrypting those two columns first requires moving that write and all three reads behind an edge route. Doing the crypto without that would lock a seller out of their own Settings page and would break the account export. iOS and Android touch neither column (grepped both trees, zero hits), so the migration surface is web-only - which makes the prerequisite tractable, just not free. AC3's migration is ALSO wrong for AC1 as written: ship_from_address is jsonb, so storing an envelope string means a type change, not just a value change. AC2 SHIPPED, and measure_card_requests is the more sensitive of the two anyway - it holds a full street address, not a ship-from region. It has none of AC1's problem: deny-all RLS (rls-guard_test.ts:181), written by exactly ONE edge route (flipdesk-measure.ts POST /card-request) and read by exactly ONE (admin-measure-cards.ts listRequests, feeding the fulfilment CSV). Both sides already run where the key lives. NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/measure-card-pii.ts encrypts ship_name, address_line1, address_line2, city and postal_code with encryptToken() and the OWNER'S USER ID AS AAD. state and country stay plaintext exactly as AC2 asks, and a test asserts the two lists cannot overlap - the export filters and sorts by region, and an equality on an encrypted column cannot use an index or match at all. AC7 IS THE CASE WORTH READING. Encrypting a column is easy to do in a way that helps nobody: one key, no binding, and anyone who can write a row can copy another tenant's ciphertext onto it and read the plaintext back through the normal decrypt path. AES-GCM covers additionalData with the auth tag, so A's address fails to decrypt under B's id. That is the US-268 property expressed in cryptography instead of in an .eq() someone has to remember, and it is asserted rather than assumed. THE WRITE ENCRYPTS BEFORE THE INSERT, not after it. An insert-then-update would leave the address readable in the WAL and in any replica that saw the first version, which is most of what a stolen-dump scenario actually covers. A key misconfiguration answers 503 rather than falling back to plaintext. THE READ USES THE ROW'S OWNER, never a caller-supplied id, and decrypts PER ROW: one un-backfilled or unreadable row must not take out the operator's whole fulfilment queue, so a failure blanks that address and logs the id. A blank that says so beats a plausible-looking wrong address on a mailing label. AC4 - TOLERANCE PLUS A BACKFILL, and the backfill is a SCRIPT because it cannot be a migration. pgcrypto offers AES in CBC/ECB only: no GCM, therefore no auth tag, therefore no AAD - a SQL backfill would produce ciphertext the edge cannot read carrying none of the security this story is about. NEW scripts/backfill-measure-card-pii.ts is DRY-RUN BY DEFAULT (--apply to write), refuses to start without EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY (encrypting under the wrong key would make every address silently unreadable while still LOOKING encrypted), and scopes its update by owner_user_id as well as id so a mis-derived id cannot write one seller's owner-bound ciphertext onto another's row, where it would be permanently undecryptable. Re-running it is a no-op: already-encrypted values pass through, so an interrupted run resumes with no bookkeeping. Double-wrapping would be UNRECOVERABLE, since the inner envelope's AAD is invisible from the outside, and a test pins that. MY OWN TEST HAD A BLIND SPOT AND THE SABOTAGE FOUND IT. The route-text check forbade `city:` in the insert, so an accidental SHORTHAND `city,` - which writes the same plaintext and overrides the spread - stayed green. Each reddened with its own message; all files restored and re-run green. THE PREREQUISITE THE LAST PASS NAMED IS BUILT. NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/user-shipping-pii.ts encrypts users.ship_from_address and users.business_phone with encryptToken() and THE ROW'S OWN ID AS AAD; NEW GET/PUT /api/account/shipping-profile in routes/account.ts is the only reader and writer; NEW src/lib/shipping-profile.ts is the only browser client; 00567_users_shipping_pii_edge_only.sql restates guard_users_protected_columns WITHOUT the two columns so a direct browser write now RAISES instead of storing plaintext over ciphertext. Better still, the JSON TYPE becomes the AC4 discriminator: an OBJECT is a row the backfill has not reached, a STRING is an envelope. No prefix sniffing on a value that could legitimately start with anything. 00567 therefore contains NO DDL at all - one CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION plus two column comments - and its risk is entirely in APPLY ORDER, which PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md spells out: apply the SQL, NOTIFY pgrst, redeploy the edge, THEN push. Pushing first ships a frontend calling a route that does not exist. AC4: NEW scripts/backfill-user-shipping-pii.ts, dry-run by default, refuses to start without EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY, re-runnable because an already-encrypted value passes through rather than double-wrapping (which is unrecoverable - the inner AAD is invisible from outside). Read tolerates both formats, so there is no deadline on running it. AC5: BOTH edge readers were found and both decrypt at the boundary - routes/account.ts and routes/flipdesk-logistics.ts (the label quote). Grepped functions/, ios/ and android/: zero hits, confirming the last pass's finding. A containment case is appended to tenant-isolation_test.ts, and the property it pins is the one that is easy to get wrong here: this endpoint reads c.get('userId') and NOT c.get('workspaceOwnerId'), because a manager inside A's workspace must not read A's home address, so the case sends X-Workspace-Owner pointed at A and asserts B's write never lands on A. userStories.notes: [P3][Cohesion/Mobile] DEFERRED 2026-06-08 — needs real device/PWA QA, and the audit was partly stale.
