userStories.title: Email-keyed PII retained for accounts deleted BEFORE the US-2005 purge shipped is still queryable
userStories.description: US-2005 added an email-keyed purge to the deletion path, so erasure is complete from that point on. It is not retroactive. Every account deleted before it shipped left its address — and in email_deliveries the full rendered html of every email we sent it — in the seven tables EMAIL_PURGE_PLAN now covers. Those users asked to be forgotten and were told {deleted:true}. The deletion log written by routes/account.ts records who was deleted and when, so the population is identifiable rather than hypothetical, which is what makes this actionable rather than a shrug.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish the population from the deletion log rather than guessing: which deletions predate the purge, and whether their addresses are still present in any planned table. Report the count BEFORE deleting anything — a backfill whose blast radius was never measured is how a cleanup becomes an incident.

Re-run the SAME plan, not a hand-written script. purgeEmailKeyedPii(address, io) already encodes which table is deleted and which anonymized; a parallel script would drift from it, which is the exact thing US-2005 spent its effort avoiding.
The run is idempotent and logged per address, so an interrupted pass resumes without re-deriving what it already did.
Record the outcome where a regulator-facing answer would be looked up, not only in this story: how many subjects, which tables, and the date the backlog reached zero.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/GDPR][OPERATOR] Filed 2026-08-08 from US-2005, which fixed the path forward and explicitly left this as a prod data task. CANNOT be done from a dev checkout: it needs the production database. The code half already exists — purgeEmailKeyedPii takes an address and an IO seam, so the operator half is a script that enumerates addresses and calls it. Pairs with US-2433; both are operator-run data tasks and would share one runbook. | 2026-08-10 THIS STORY'S PREMISE IS FALSE AND THE BACKFILL IT ASKS FOR MUST NOT BE RUN. The description says "The deletion log written by routes/account.ts records who was deleted and when, so the population is identifiable rather than hypothetical". It does not. Three facts, each read off the schema rather than assumed: (1) account_deletion_log HOLDS NO ADDRESS, deliberately — migration 00064's own header says the retained id is "opaque, no-longer-resolvable ... it cannot be joined back to any PII". It proves THAT an account id was erased on a date; it cannot say WHOSE address that was. That was the right call for a compliance record and it is precisely what makes this backfill impossible. (2) email_deliveries — the worst table, the one holding the full rendered html — HAS NO user_id COLUMN AT ALL (00095). Nothing to join, not even a severed link. (3) Every other planned table either severs its user link ON DELETE SET NULL (marketing_send_log.owner_user_id, email_subscribers.user_id, waitlist_entries.user_id) or never had one of its own (email_journey_step_sends). So NULL means "account deleted" OR "never had an account" and nothing distinguishes them. THE DANGEROUS PART IS NOT THAT AC1 IS UNANSWERABLE, IT IS THAT A PROXY LOOKS RIGHT. "An address in a planned table with no live account" reads like the population and is mostly the WRONG PEOPLE: waitlist_entries and email_subscribers exist for people who never had an account, by definition. Running EMAIL_PURGE_PLAN over that set deletes the waitlist and the newsletter list, for subjects who never asked to be forgotten, on the theory that some of them might be someone else. AC1's own warning — "a backfill whose blast radius was never measured is how a cleanup becomes an incident" — is the right instinct aimed at the wrong risk: the danger is not the SIZE of the set, it is that it is the wrong set. SHIPPED INSTEAD, three things. (a) src/lib/email-residue-census.ts + scripts/email-residue-census.ts: counts distinct addresses per planned table, split into live_account and unattributable, driven off EMAIL_PURGE_PLAN so it cannot drift from the plan. There is NO deleted_account bucket and no delete path, and both absences are pinned by tests — a bucket named after a group it cannot identify is how a census becomes a work list. The script has no --apply and never will. It never prints or returns an address, asserted against the STRUCTURE as well as the rendering, because the string check alone passes trivially today and would keep passing if someone added a samples field "for debugging". censusNotes() ships the sentences that must travel with the numbers, as data rather than print statements, so a future admin surface says the same thing. (b) scripts/purge-email-subject.ts: the case that actually arises. A subject writes in, so the address is known and no inference is involved. Calls purgeEmailKeyedPii — the SAME plan the live endpoint runs, which is AC2 in one line. Idempotent by construction (AC3): every operation is delete-by-address or null-by-address, so a second run matches nothing and succeeds; there is no cursor to lose. Dry run by default, and it REFUSES an address belonging to a live account — running the plan on one would delete a current customer's newsletter subscription and waitlist row without deleting their account, a half-erasure nobody asked for and the easiest mistake to make off a support ticket. NOT AN ENDPOINT, the same call US-2433 made: a route that erases on an unverified email claim is a deletion oracle. (c) AC4: vault/10-ops/data-retention.md now carries the whole thing under "Deletion (right to erasure)" — the email-keyed purge itself (which that runbook never mentioned even though US-2005 shipped months ago), the suppression exemption, and a section headed "What we can and cannot say about erasures made before US-2005" giving the answer to hand a regulator. SECOND FINDING, WHICH SHRINKS THE PROBLEM: US-2021 already put email_deliveries on the retention sweep — sent rows DELETED after 90 days, dead_letter bodies stripped after 180 (data-retention.ts:191-240). The largest reservoir this story names is therefore draining on its own, and the story does not know it. Conditional on the data-retention cron actually being scheduled in prod, which this checkout cannot see and which is exactly the US-2002 failure class. So the census reads cron_runs for the last successful data-retention tick and says plainly when there is none, because if the sweep is not running every count is growing rather than draining and reading it as stable would be wrong. STAYS passes:false, and the reason has changed rather than shrunk: nobody has RUN the census (AC1 asks for the count, and that needs prod), and AC2/AC3's bulk form is not merely undone but unachievable — what exists is the per-request path. Whoever picks this up next should re-scope the ACs rather than look for the missing script. VERIFIED: deno check clean on all three new files and on src/main.ts, deno lint clean across 1480 files, full edge suite 6419 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (+15), vault:index up to date, vault:lint --strict clean across 164 notes. Negative-verified 9 ways, each reddening its own named test: row counts instead of distinct people, the notes dropping the 00064 citation, the do-not-run warning softened, a stopped retention cron reporting as fine, sample addresses kept for debugging, a delete path added to the census module, an --apply added to the census script, the purge no longer refusing a live account, and the census inventing its own table list. TWO OF MY OWN MUTATIONS WERE WRONG BEFORE THE CODE WAS: one broke type-checking rather than a test, and one "leaked" a value the structure cannot hold — the leak test was VACUOUS as first written and is now asserted against JSON.stringify(census), which is falsifiable.

userStories.title: `npm run verify` failed for anyone with the local Supabase stack running — eslint was linting generated stack files
userStories.description: FIXED 2026-08-08 in the same pass that found it; filed so the fix is discoverable and so the class is on record. `supabase start` writes a generated, minified edge-runtime bundle to supabase/.temp/start-secrets/. That directory was not gitignored (only the single file supabase/.temp/cli-latest was, listed FOUR times) and was not in eslint's ignore list, so `npm run lint` — and therefore `npm run verify` — reported 189 errors in code nobody wrote. CI never sees it, because the web lane does not run `supabase start`. The people it broke are exactly the ones following CLAUDE.md: the tenant-isolation and money-cert suites both require the full local stack, so anyone who ran those and then ran verify got a wall of errors in minified output and no indication it was not their change.
acceptanceCriteria: DONE: .gitignore ignores supabase/.temp/ as a DIRECTORY, replacing four copies of a line that covered one file inside it.
DONE: eslint.config.js ignores supabase/.temp/** with the reason written at the ignore.

OPEN: supabase/.temp/cli-latest is TRACKED in git and also gitignored, which is why it shows as modified in every working tree that has ever booted the local stack. Ignoring a tracked file does nothing. It should be `git rm --cached`-ed, but that changes what is committed and is the owner's call, not a side effect of a lint fix.

OPEN: decide whether verify should FAIL when it lints a path that is gitignored. This bug was invisible until someone happened to run verify with the stack up; a check that the lint target set and the git-tracked set agree would have caught it on the first run.
userStories.notes: [P3][DX/CI] Found 2026-08-08 while running `npm run verify` to check a session's accumulated work, with the local Supabase stack up for the migration testing. The first two ACs were fixed on the spot; after the fix `node scripts/verify.mjs --web` is 11/11 checks and `--edge` is 4/4. THE THIRD AC IS THE INTERESTING ONE. A file that is both TRACKED and GITIGNORED is a state git gives no warning about: the ignore silently does nothing, and the file keeps appearing as modified forever. supabase/.temp/cli-latest has been in that state long enough that four separate ignore lines were added for it, each presumably by someone who saw it dirty and assumed it just needed ignoring. That is the tell — a rule added four times is a rule that never worked. | Done 2026-08-08. AC4 SHIPPED as scripts/check-tracked-ignored.mjs, wired into verify.mjs (web lane, BEFORE eslint so the cause is named before the wall of symptoms) and into ci.yml, so a --no-verify push cannot shed it. It runs one git call — `git ls-files --cached --ignored --exclude-standard` — and fails on any path not in its KNOWN baseline, and equally on a KNOWN entry that has LEFT the state, so the list can only shrink (the KNOWN_UNREACHABLE_CRONS pattern from cron-registry-drift_test.ts). Both directions negative-verified. THE STORY UNDERSTATED THE PROBLEM BY 33x. AC3 describes supabase/.temp/cli-latest as the tracked-and-gitignored file; measured, there are 32, and they are not one class but three, with three different correct fixes — which is exactly why the guard reports and refuses to guess: (1) services/edge-functions/deno.lock — THE IGNORE WAS THE BUG, NOT THE TRACKING, and this one I fixed outright because it changes nothing about what is committed. It was line 101 of .gitignore, uncommented, in a block of Ralph runtime junk. The lockfile is tracked and MUST stay tracked: US-517's `deno cache --frozen src/main.ts` gate (verify.mjs + security.yml) exists to fail the build when a resolved dependency drifts, and a frozen check with no committed lockfile has nothing to freeze against. Deleted the line with the reasoning written at it. Verified after: git check-ignore exits 1 (no longer ignored), the file is still tracked, deno cache --frozen still exits 0. (2) temp_prd/** — 20 loose OOXML parts of an unzipped FlipDesk_PRD_v1.docx, committed and then ignored as a directory. (3) assets/hf_*.mp4|png, an ios-screenshots PNG, and a .pyc — generated media and build debris committed before their ignore rules landed. Groups 2 and 3 plus cli-latest are baselined with the decision each is waiting on, because `git rm --cached` changes what a fresh clone receives and that is the owner's call, not a side effect of a lint fix — the same reason AC3 gives. AC3 THEREFORE STAYS OPEN AS A DECISION, but it is no longer invisible: it is 31 named paths in a file CI reads, instead of a sentence in a backlog note. AC1/AC2 confirmed still in place (.gitignore ignores supabase/.temp/ as a directory; eslint.config.js ignores supabase/.temp/** with the reason written at the ignore). VERIFIED: check-tracked-ignored clean at 32 known, npm run lint 0 errors, npx tsc -b clean, deno cache --frozen clean. ⚠ SEPARATE FINDING, NOT PART OF THIS STORY, found while reading .gitignore: line 95 ignores supabase/migrations/00122_verified_storefront_listings.sql. That migration was never committed (git log --all finds nothing) and is absent from the working tree — 00121 and 00123 are both present, so the sequence has a hole. The ignore line was added by 645cd1f3, the commit that shipped the storefront-listings feature itself. Filed separately. | REOPENED IMMEDIATELY, same session, and the mistake is worth recording. I flipped this to passes:true on the strength of AC4 shipping, while my own note in the same breath said 'AC3 THEREFORE STAYS OPEN AS A DECISION'. Two ACs done and one open is passes:false — an AC that needs the owner rather than an agent is still an unmet AC, not an exemption. This is the US-1996 failure mode (a story marked done while an explicitly deferred criterion is outstanding) committed by the very session that was working the backlog, which is how it keeps happening. AC3 is the ONLY thing outstanding: 31 tracked-and-gitignored paths need a per-path keep-or-untrack call. They are enumerated in scripts/check-tracked-ignored.mjs KNOWN, grouped by the fix each needs, and CI now reads that file — so the decision is visible instead of buried.

userStories.title: Web lost the AI listing-copy button that iOS ships and settings.tsx still promises
userStories.description: Found while triaging dead exports in US-2436. src/hooks/use-ai-extract.ts exported useListingCopy, a mutation posting to /api/flipdesk/ai/listing-copy, and nothing on the web has called it for some time. It is not dead work: the edge route is live (routes/flipdesk-ai.ts -> lib/ai-extract.ts generateListingCopy) and iOS calls it from Marketplaces/Publish/ListingCopyService.swift. Meanwhile src/pages/settings.tsx tells the user, in the AI toggle copy, that turning the setting off disables the AI Fill and listing-copy buttons — naming a web button that is not there. The composer does generate copy, but through a different endpoint entirely (useAiRewrite -> /api/flipdesk/ai/rewrite), so the two are not the same feature under a different name. US-2436 deliberately left the hook in place rather than delete it, because deleting it would have quietly ratified the gap.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide first whether the web is meant to have this at all, given the composer already rewrites copy through /api/flipdesk/ai/rewrite. If rewrite has genuinely superseded it on the web, that is a legitimate answer — then delete useListingCopy and fix the settings string.
If it is meant to exist, wire it somewhere a seller can reach and check it counts against the same AI-action quota the route already enforces.
Either way src/pages/settings.tsx must stop describing a button that is not on the page. That sentence is the part actively lying to a user today and it is cheap to fix on its own.
Do not delete the edge route or generateListingCopy under any outcome — iOS is a live consumer.
userStories.notes: [P3][Web/Parity] Filed 2026-08-08 out of US-2436. The settings-copy fix and the wiring decision are separable — AC3 alone is worth shipping even if the rest waits. Related: US-2361 covers the other intended-but-unadopted hook found in the same pass, useFeatureFlag. | 2026-08-08 AC3 DONE — the sentence that was actively lying is fixed. settings.tsx said 'When off, AI Fill and listing-copy buttons are disabled account-wide', naming a listing-copy button the web does not have. That reads to a seller as the SETTING being broken rather than the copy being wrong, which is why it was worth shipping ahead of the wiring decision. REWRITTEN BY WHAT THE WEB ACTUALLY HAS, and deliberately NOT as another list of buttons: the toggle gates EVERY /api/flipdesk/ai/* route server-side — flipdesk-ai.ts checks ai_enrichment_enabled in the shared quota helper before extract, extract-aspects, size, listing-copy, rewrite, bulk-extract, embed-photos and classify-photos alike. Enumerating a subset is exactly what let this drift, so the copy now says every AI feature is disabled and names three as examples rather than as the set. LEFT ALONE ON PURPOSE: the CardDescription's 'writes listing copy from your descriptions and photos'. That one is TRUE on the web — the composer's rewrite actions include description_regen and title_seo, which is writing listing copy. It describes a capability rather than a control, so it is not the thing that misleads. AC1/AC2 REMAIN AND ARE A PRODUCT CALL I did not make for you, though the evidence is now gathered: /api/flipdesk/ai/rewrite offers title_seo, title_shorten, title_keywords, description_tighten and description_regen, which functionally covers what listing-copy does, and the composer already exposes them. So 'rewrite has superseded it on the web' is a defensible answer to AC1 — but it is a decision about what the product offers, not a cleanup, so useListingCopy stays until someone makes it. AC4 is untouched and must stay so: the edge route and generateListingCopy have a live iOS consumer (Marketplaces/Publish/ListingCopyService.swift). Story stays passes:false on AC1/AC2. VERIFIED: tsc -b clean, eslint clean, 810 web guard tests pass.

userStories.title: Migration 00122 is gitignored and was never committed — the migration sequence has a hole and no fresh environment can reach prod's schema
userStories.description: supabase/migrations/00122_verified_storefront_listings.sql is named explicitly in .gitignore (line 95) and does not exist in the working tree or anywhere in git history (`git log --all -- 'supabase/migrations/00122*'` returns nothing). 00121 and 00123 are both present, so the sequence has a hole at exactly one number. The ignore line was added by 645cd1f3, the same commit that shipped the storefront-listings feature — so whatever DDL that feature needs was applied to prod by hand and then deliberately kept out of the repo. Consequences: the verify:db lane resets a throwaway stack from supabase/migrations/ and therefore proves migrations apply on a fresh schema that is NOT prod's schema; any new environment built from the repo is missing the objects; and EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION (00563) counts a file nobody can read. This is the inverse of the usual drift — normally the repo is ahead of prod.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish what 00122 actually did. The storefront feature is live, so the objects exist in prod: read them out of the running database (information_schema / pg_dump of the relevant tables, policies and functions) rather than reconstructing from the feature commit's application code, which only shows what it EXPECTED.

Decide whether the ignore was protecting something. A migration excluded on purpose usually means it carried a secret, an environment-specific value, or a destructive one-off. If that is the case the answer is a sanitised replacement, not un-ignoring the original — and the reason goes in the file.

Restore a committed migration covering those objects, idempotent per the US-1108 triple (idempotent SQL / EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bump in the SAME commit / self-record footer). It must be safe to apply to a prod that ALREADY has the objects — that is the whole reason it has to be idempotent rather than a plain CREATE.
Remove the .gitignore line, and confirm no other migration is ignored: `git check-ignore supabase/migrations/*.sql` must match nothing.

Add a guard so a migration can never be gitignored again — the sequence-gap and the ignore are each independently checkable, and neither was checked. Fold it into the migrations lint rather than a new one-off script.
userStories.notes: [P1][DB/Drift] Found 2026-08-08 while working US-2437 AC4 (the tracked-and-gitignored guard) — reading .gitignore top to bottom for that check is what surfaced it; nothing was looking for it. EVIDENCE, all measured: .gitignore:95 names the file; `ls supabase/migrations/ | grep 00122` is empty; `git ls-files` is empty; `git log --all --oneline -- 'supabase/migrations/00122*'` is empty (never committed, not deleted later); 00120, 00121, 00123, 00124 all present; `git log -S 00122_verified_storefront_listings -- .gitignore` points at 645cd1f3 'feat(storefront): implement storefront listings feature for verified profiles'. P1 because it silently invalidates a safety net rather than breaking a feature: verify:db and the db-migrations CI lane both exist to prove migrations apply to a FRESH schema, and they have been proving it against a schema that is missing an object prod has. Nobody would notice until a restore, a new environment, or a migration that assumes 00122's objects exist. NOT urgent in the user-facing sense — storefront listings work in prod, which is precisely why this survived. | 2026-08-08 AC4 and AC5 DONE; AC1-AC3 stay open because they need a read of the running database, which no checkout can do. AC4: the .gitignore line naming 00122 is gone, replaced by a comment recording why the hole was invisible; `git check-ignore supabase/migrations/*.sql` now matches nothing. Removing the line does NOT restore the file and the comment says so - it restores the ability to notice. AC5 SHIPPED as scripts/migrations-lint.mjs, wired into BOTH scripts/verify.mjs (web lane) and .github/workflows/ci.yml. Four rules, each of which was independently checkable and none of which was checked: (1) no ignore rule may reach supabase/migrations/ - two halves, because they catch different mistakes: git check-ignore over every entry plus two probe paths, AND a literal read of .gitignore / .git/info/exclude / a nested supabase/migrations/.gitignore. The second half is the one that finds a 00122: a rule written against a filename that does not exist yet matches nothing on disk, so no scan of the directory can ever see it. (2) filename shape NNNNN_snake_case.sql, 5 or 6 digits. (3) no two migrations share a schema_migrations version. (4) sequence gaps against an annotated KNOWN_GAPS map that may only shrink. NOT IN db-migrations.yml, deliberately: that workflow is path-filtered to supabase/migrations/**, and the change that lost 00122 was a .gitignore edit, which would not have triggered it. Same reason it is in the web lane rather than the Docker-gated db lane - the bug is invisible to a check that applies the files present. THE SEQUENCE HAS FIVE GAPS, NOT ONE, and measuring them is what made the baseline usable: 00011, 00014 and 00479 were never authored (no file in any commit), 00527 is 00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED where the suffix IS the safety mechanism (US-2403), and 00122 is this story. A bare list of numbers would have been unshrinkable, so every entry carries its reason and a test asserts each reason is non-trivial. TWO THINGS I EXPECTED TO BE BUGS AND WERE NOT, checked rather than assumed. The three 6-digit filenames (000355_photo_types_v2, 000375_push_device_tokens, 000385_feedback_messages) look like a numbering error and are the opposite: commit e4a44545 split three duplicate-prefix pairs, and 000355 sorts lexically between 00035 and 00036, so apply order is preserved exactly. They are pinned in SIX_DIGIT_BY_DESIGN and a NEW 6-digit name now fails, because it would mean the collision recurred - that collision broke `supabase db start` outright with a duplicate-key error naming a Postgres constraint rather than a file, which is why rule 3 exists at all. ONE REAL SUBTLETY: git check-ignore reports NOTHING for a tracked path by default, so an ignore rule added over the existing migrations read as clean until --no-index went in. Found by negative verification, not by review. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED SEVEN WAYS end to end: an ignore rule over an existing migration, an ignore rule matching only future files, a malformed filename, a duplicate version, a new gap, a stale KNOWN_GAPS entry, and a missing pinned 6-digit file - each reddened its own case and was restored. 17 cases in NEW scripts/migrations-lint.test.mjs, all against SYNTHETIC directories rather than the real one: a test asserting 'the repo passes today' goes green forever the moment the repo is clean and never proves the rules would fire. Six source mutations confirm that (SHAPE widened, nested-ignore handling dropped, the unexplained filter stubbed, the filled filter stubbed, duplicate detection stubbed, the pinned-but-absent push removed) - each reddened, module restored. STILL OPEN AND ALL OWNER WORK: AC1 (read 00122's objects out of prod via information_schema/pg_dump, not reconstructed from 645cd1f3's application code, which shows what it EXPECTED), AC2 (decide whether the ignore was protecting a secret or an environment-specific value, in which case the answer is a sanitised replacement), AC3 (commit an idempotent migration safe to apply to a prod that already has the objects, per the US-1108 triple). userStories.title: The edge hang watchdog did not cap the outage at ~60s, and nothing in the repo can tell whether it is still installed
userStories.description: As the operator, I want the edge-hang safety net verified from the repo, so that a watchdog that has stopped running is discovered before the next hang rather than during it. MEASURED 2026-08-09 from outside, against the public hostname, with no host access: /health/ready answered normally at ~19:06 UTC; at 19:19 requests hung to a full 25s timeout (http=000); at 19:22 both /health and /health/ready were unreachable while gradethread.com returned 200 and api.gradethread.com answered — the exact edge-hang signature; at 19:27 it settled into a fast 503 with the body 'no available server' (Traefik's, meaning the backend was pulled from the pool); it recovered by 19:39. That is AT LEAST ~8 minutes of confirmed failure inside a 33-minute window, against a watchdog that vault/10-ops/edge-hang-vs-crash-loop.md says restarts on unhealthy every minute and 'caps the outage at ~60s'. Grading, payments, eBay writes and Stripe webhooks were all dead for that window while the marketing site and login stayed up — the failure mode that note records as having cost four weeks the first time.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish by MEASUREMENT whether /opt/gradethread/edge-watchdog.sh exists on the host and is actually scheduled (crontab -l), and record the finding either way in vault/10-ops/edge-hang-vs-crash-loop.md. From outside there is no way to distinguish a late watchdog from an absent one, so this cannot be inferred.

If it is missing or not scheduled: restore it, and PROVE the cap by inducing an unhealthy container on a non-production copy and observing the restart, rather than by reading the crontab. The claim being repaired is a timing claim.

The watchdog's existence becomes checkable WITHOUT SSH — its script and schedule live in the repo (or in the schedule artifact US-2313 defines), so its absence is detectable by a check rather than by an outage.

The ~60s cap in vault/10-ops/edge-hang-vs-crash-loop.md is corrected to whatever is measured, or the note states plainly that the cap is unverified. The 2026-08-09 timings are already recorded there and must not be removed — a second occurrence is the evidence.

An alert fires to a human when the public /health/ready is unreachable for longer than the cap, independent of the watchdog itself. A safety net that is also the only detector cannot report its own failure.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-11 AC3, AC4 and AC5 DONE. AC1 and AC2 are the operator's and cannot be faked from a checkout. THE PROBLEM RESTATED, because the fix only makes sense against it: three states looked IDENTICAL from outside on 2026-08-09 — the watchdog fired late, the watchdog failed, the watchdog was uninstalled months ago. Nothing in the repo could tell them apart, and the only thing that ever reported the answer was the next outage, which is the moment nobody can go and look. AC3 SHIPPED IN FOUR PIECES. (1) scripts/ops/edge-watchdog.sh — the script itself, in version control for the first time, LF-pinned by the existing *.sh gitattributes rule (a CRLF shebang on a cron job is a SILENT no-op, i.e. this exact invisible-absence reintroduced by a line ending). It defers to Docker's own health verdict, and treats an EMPTY health status as 'no healthcheck configured' rather than unhealthy, because restarting on that is a reboot loop. (2) scripts/ops/host-schedules.json — the schedule as data, including the exact crontab line an operator pastes. DELIBERATELY SCOPED TO HOST SCHEDULES ONLY and the file says so: the ~74 EDGE crons have their own registry (CRON_REGISTRY) and US-2313 owns making those verifiable. Two half-registries that disagree is the shape this repo keeps relearning, and folding them here would also read as US-2313 being done. (3) POST /api/jobs/watchdog-heartbeat — the script checks in every minute; the timestamp lands in system_settings ops.edge_watchdog_last_seen, so NO MIGRATION. (4) GET /health/ready reports it as checks.features.hostWatchdog. WHY THAT IS THE ANSWER TO AC3 AND NOT A PROXY FOR IT: the absence now shows up during NORMAL operation, off-host, instead of during an incident. PROD WILL REPORT 'unconfigured' UNTIL THE OPERATOR INSTALLS IT, and that is the correct output rather than a rollout wart — the true state today IS unknown, and an entry saying so is strictly better than the silence it replaces. Same posture US-2001 took with release='dev'. TWO LIMITS STATED IN THE CODE RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE DISCOVERED: the heartbeat travels THROUGH the service the watchdog protects, so it cannot report during the very outage it bounds — it answers the steady-state question, which is the one that was unanswerable; and it still does not verify the ~60s cap, which is a TIMING claim and needs AC2's induced-unhealthy test on a non-production copy. AC5 was already satisfied by uptime.yml + uptime-check.mjs; what is new is that the probe now surfaces hostWatchdog as a NOTE that can never flip up/down. Paging on it would fire every ten minutes forever until the install happens, and a muted monitor is worse than none — but it rides along on the FAILING line too, which is the moment 'was the watchdog even running?' is the first question anyone asks. AC4: the vault warning block previously said the script 'is not in this repo... so nothing in the checkout can tell you whether it is still installed'. That sentence is now false, so it is quoted as the thing that was true and replaced, rather than deleted — the 2026-08-09 timings stay exactly as AC4 requires. GUARDS: scripts/host-schedules.test.mjs (10 cases, pins manifest/script/crontab agreement, the LF shebang, the Docker-verdict deference, the heartbeat wiring and the staleness number in both places) and services/edge-functions/src/tests/watchdog-heartbeat_test.ts (4 BEHAVIOURAL cases) plus 5 new health_test.ts cases. ⚠ ONE SABOTAGE PROVED NOTHING FIRST TIME AND THAT IS THE REUSABLE PART: disabling the secret gate to 'if (false)' left both the strings 'requireJobSecret' and '401' in the file, so my token-search assertion stayed GREEN over a dead gate. A dead gate and a live one are indistinguishable to a token search. Replaced with a pinned whole-branch regex, a gate-before-write ordering assertion, AND the behavioural test that actually calls the handler with no secret, a wrong secret and an empty configured secret. That mattered here specifically: an unauthenticated writer could forge a heartbeat and make an absent watchdog read as healthy, turning the detector into a source of false confidence — worse than the blind spot it fills. SIX SABOTAGES in total, each reddening its own case: manifest cron disagreeing with the crontab line, the script restarting without asking Docker, the gate disabled (reddens 3 behavioural cases AND the strengthened scan), the uptime note starting to decide up/down, readiness gating on the feature map, and health.ts re-spelling the settings key instead of importing it. AC1 AND AC2 REMAIN AND ARE OPERATOR WORK: confirm the script is present and on cron (crontab -l), then PROVE the cap by inducing an unhealthy container on a non-production copy and timing the restart. The claim being repaired is a timing claim; a crontab read cannot establish it. VERIFIED: test:scripts 386 passed / 20 files, health_test.ts 22 passed (5 new), watchdog-heartbeat_test.ts 4 passed (new), deno lint clean across 1503 files, deno check clean on main.ts, vault:lint --strict clean at 172 notes. NO MIGRATION — the heartbeat rides an existing system_settings row. | THE DRIFT GUARD CAUGHT THE NEW ROUTE, and the fix is the part worth reading. cron-registry-drift_test.ts asserts every /api/jobs/* route in main.ts has a CRON_REGISTRY entry, and mine did not — correctly, since I had added one. But REGISTERING it would have been wrong: CRON_REGISTRY drives the operator docs (COOLIFY.md and launch-checklist.md embed renderCronDocs() verbatim), so every entry reads as 'create this task in the Coolify UI', and this endpoint is called by a HOST cron. An entry would have instructed the operator to build a second, duplicate scheduler. Exempted instead, with the escape hatch closed: a new test asserts any exempted endpoint APPEARS in scripts/ops/host-schedules.json, so the exemption can only MOVE a route from one registry to the other and can never leave it unregistered. Negative-verified — deleting the manifest's heartbeat block reddens that case.

userStories.title: Every control in a FlipDesk listings row is named the same thing, so a screen reader cannot tell which garment it is about to reprice
userStories.description: US-2335 ground the unlabelled-control count to zero and the listings table passed that bar the whole time: every inline editor announced "Edit value", the status control "Change status", the checkbox "Select row", the delete button "Delete item". Those are names, so the audit counted them as fixed. But the table renders up to a few hundred virtualized rows with roughly fourteen controls each, and a screen reader user moving down a column hears the same four words repeatedly with nothing identifying the item. A name that does not distinguish is not a usable name, which is the exact caveat src/test/control-labels.test.ts records under AC4 and the exact case the count cannot measure. A second, quieter defect sits in the same rows: the row's own activate label read it.item_title ?? it.listing_title, skipping the US-1569 placeholder fallback that the visible title cell applies, so a row DISPLAYING "Nike Windbreaker" announced itself as "Open Item 42".
acceptanceCriteria: Every per-row control in src/pages/flipdesk/listings-table.tsx names its own row, so two rows never announce identically.
The row name comes from one shared derivation, and the visible title cell uses the same rule, so the spoken and printed titles cannot drift apart again.
An untitled row still gets a distinguishing name: no shared constant fallback, because fresh drafts are exactly the rows most likely to be untitled and would all collapse onto it.
The row identity is a REQUIRED prop on InlineCell and InlineStatusSelect, so the compiler refuses a new call site that forgets it.
A guard fails the build if a fixed-string aria-label reappears inside a row, with a short allowlist for the genuinely table-level controls.
AC4-of-US-2335 still open here: nobody has driven this table with a real screen reader. Distinguishing names are necessary and not sufficient.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-10 AC1-AC5 DONE, AC6 open and it is the honest one. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG: not a missing name anywhere. Every control in a listings row already had one, which is why US-2335's count read zero on this file the whole time; they were all the SAME name. Seven "Edit value" editors, "Change status", "Select row", "Open full editor", "Delete item", "Open listing", "End listing early", "Relist as a new listing", plus Sold / Mark / Publish / List it / Mark shipped / Mark delivered naming themselves off their visible text. Roughly fourteen per row, across up to a few hundred virtualized rows. NEW MODULE src/lib/item-row-label.ts holds three functions: itemDisplayTitle (the US-1569 placeholder fallback, moved verbatim out of the JSX), itemRowLabel (never empty, never shared) and rowControlLabel. Derived ONCE per row in listings-table.tsx, not per control, so the row cannot introduce itself one way to the checkbox and another way to the price editor. THE FALLBACK CHAIN IS THE INTERESTING PART: itemRowLabel deliberately REFUSES a placeholder title that itemDisplayTitle happily returns. A draft titled "Item 42" with no generated listing title yet should still DISPLAY "Item 42" (that is what the cell did before and changing it would be a silent visual change), but speaking it is wrong, because "Untitled draft" is what every fresh draft is called and a screen of them would all get the same name — the defect, rebuilt, for exactly the rows most likely to hit it. So placeholder falls through to item_number and then to an 8-char id slice. Ugly to hear, distinguishing, and that is the job. DELIBERATELY NOT TRUNCATED: an eBay title runs to 80 chars and two listings often differ only in the size or colourway at the END, so a truncated label would make them announce identically. A label is read once on focus; length costs less than ambiguity. THE COMPILER IS THE GUARD, not a test: rowLabel is a REQUIRED prop on both InlineCell and InlineStatusSelect (label too, on InlineCell). Optional would have been the polite choice and it would have been forgotten. The source-scanning test is the backstop for the shortcut the type cannot catch — passing a literal to satisfy it — plus a scan that fails on any fixed-string aria-label in the file outside a two-entry table-level allowlist. SECOND DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, unnamed in the story when filed: ClickableRow's activateLabel read `it.item_title ?? it.listing_title`, skipping the US-1569 fallback the title cell applies two lines below it, so a row DISPLAYING "Nike Windbreaker" announced itself "Open Item 42". That is why the visible cell now calls itemDisplayTitle too — one rule, one place. activateLabel is not an aria-label attribute so the fixed-label scan cannot see it; it has its own assertion. OUT OF SCOPE ON PURPOSE: the "Queue" link in the drafts column. Its target is a publish BATCH shared by many rows, so naming it after one item would be actively wrong, and the batch has no human-readable name to use instead. Left alone rather than given a plausible-sounding label. AC6 IS NOT A FORMALITY: nobody has driven this table with a real screen reader. Distinguishing names are necessary and not sufficient — a correct name can still be announced at the wrong moment, and fourteen controls per row is a lot of speech per item however well each one is named. That is the same gap US-2335 AC4 records, and this story does not close it. VERIFIED: npx tsc -b clean, npm run lint 0 errors / 13 warnings (unchanged), npm run ui:check 0 blocking 0/0 noise, full web suite 320 files 3916 passed 0 failed (+24), npm run build green through the 216-route prerender, prd-lint OK. Negative-verified 8 ways, each reddening its own named test and only its own: a fixed aria-label back in a row, an InlineCell handed a literal instead of its row, the activate label drifting off the helper, the placeholder rule inlined into the JSX again, the id fallback removed, a placeholder accepted as a name, the label truncated, and tagAttrs reverted.

userStories.title: Buyer audit rows are indistinguishable from seller ones, so the reconciler reads a buyer cancellation as a seller cancellation
userStories.description: Found 2026-08-10 by a sweep for remaining buyer/seller asymmetries, and it is partly a regression introduced the same day. flipdesk_subscription_events is the audit table for BOTH products - App Store and Play rows have always been namespaced (appstore., googleplay.) - but the buyer rows added by US-2119/2451/2452/2453 carried the RAW Stripe event type. reconciliation_candidates (migration 00217) is DISTINCT ON (e.user_id) with no product filter, so the newest row wins whichever product it belongs to, and it returns only event_type, to_plan and raw_payload->>status. deriveExpectedState then maps customer.subscription.deleted to {canceled, free} and invoice.payment_failed to {past_due, toPlan} and detectDivergence compares that against the SELLER cached columns. So a seller in good standing who cancels their buyer plan is flagged status_divergence, and a buyer whose card fails puts that seller in the operator dunning queue. The remedy for that flag is a resync that can overwrite flipdesk_subscription_id with the buyer subscription id, after which a plan change would push a FlipDesk price onto their Guard/Connoisseur subscription. A false flag on this queue is not noise, it is a loaded destructive action.
acceptanceCriteria: Every buyer row written to flipdesk_subscription_events is namespaced so it cannot be read as a seller signal, matching the appstore./googleplay. convention already in use.
detectDivergence refuses to compare a buyer event against the seller cached state, and says why rather than deriving something plausible.
A test asserts every buyer write site is namespaced, discovered from the source rather than listed, so a new buyer audit row cannot ship raw.

OPEN / NOT AGENT WORK: buyer subscriptions are not reconciled at all - CachedSubscriptionState has no buyer columns and the 00217 RPC selects none - so a dropped buyer webhook drifts permanently with nothing detecting it. Skipping is strictly better than a wrong flag, but it is a gap and needs its own reconciliation pass.

OPEN / NOT AGENT WORK: the resync remedy (admin-billing pickRelevantSubscription) lists subscriptions by customer with NO product filter, and buyer and seller share one Stripe customer - so it can select the buyer subscription and write its id into flipdesk_subscription_id. That is destructive and predates this story.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-10 AC1, AC2 and AC3 DONE. AC4 and AC5 stay open and are NOT agent work - they are named on this story so the sweep that found them is not lost. PART OF THIS IS A REGRESSION I INTRODUCED TODAY, and that is the first thing to say. US-2119, US-2451, US-2452 and US-2453 added buyer audit rows to flipdesk_subscription_events carrying the RAW Stripe event type. App Store and Play rows have always been namespaced (appstore., googleplay.); I did not follow the convention because I did not know the table was read by anything other than an operator. IT IS. reconciliation_candidates (migration 00217) is DISTINCT ON (e.user_id) with no product filter, and returns only event_type, to_plan and raw_payload->>status. So the newest row wins whichever product it belongs to, deriveExpectedState maps customer.subscription.deleted to {canceled, free} and invoice.payment_failed to {past_due, toPlan}, and detectDivergence compares that against the SELLER cached columns. Net effect: a seller in good standing who cancelled their BUYER plan would be flagged status_divergence, and a buyer whose card failed would put that seller into the operator dunning queue. WHY THAT IS WORSE THAN NOISE: the operator remedy for such a flag is a resync which - per AC5, pre-existing - lists subscriptions by CUSTOMER with no product filter, and buyer and seller share one Stripe customer. So it can select the buyer subscription and write its id into flipdesk_subscription_id, after which a plan change would push a FlipDesk price onto that person's Guard or Connoisseur subscription. A false flag on this queue is a loaded destructive action, not a stray line. AC1: every buyer write is namespaced through buyerEventType() - the cancellation row, the renewal receipt, the dunning and bank-challenge rows, the advance-notice row (conditionally, since handleInvoiceUpcoming serves both products from one call) and the in-place consent artifact in payments.ts. The consent artifact was BENIGN for divergence (its type is not in deriveExpectedState's vocabulary) and namespaced anyway, because it still DISPLACES the seller's genuine latest event in a distinct-on-user query and silently stops reconciling that seller until their next event. AC2: detectDivergence now refuses a buyer event with the same shape as the existing comp short-circuit, and returns expected {null,null} rather than deriving something plausible - there is no buyer column in CachedSubscriptionState to have compared against, so there is nothing honest to say. SKIPPING RATHER THAN RECONCILING IS THE DELIBERATE CHOICE: it means a buyer drift goes undetected, which is a gap, but a silent gap is strictly better than a confident wrong flag whose remedy is destructive. AC3: the guard derives the buyer write sites from source rather than listing them, so a new buyer audit row cannot ship raw. SIX SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the cancellation row un-namespaced, the dunning row un-namespaced, the shared upcoming handler no longer branching, the consent artifact un-namespaced, the detectDivergence skip removed, and the skip widened to swallow SELLER events too - which correctly reddens THREE pre-existing reconciliation tests as well as mine, and that is the half worth having: a skip that ate real seller signals would be a much more expensive fix than the flag it prevented. ⚠ ONE MUTATION PROVED NOTHING FIRST TIME and the harness lesson is now twice-learned. Writing the skip as `if (true)` made the file fail TYPE CHECKING (unreachable code), so deno test never ran, and my parser reported NOTHING FAILED because it only looked for '... FAILED' lines and for 'error: TS'. A malformed sabotage is indistinguishable from a weak guard unless the harness can tell a compile failure from a test pass. Rewritten as a mutation that compiles, and the detector now recognises 'Type checking failed' too. AC4 OPEN - BUYER SUBSCRIPTIONS ARE NOT RECONCILED AT ALL. CachedSubscriptionState has no buyer columns and the 00217 RPC selects none, so a dropped buyer webhook drifts permanently with nothing detecting it. That is the revenue leak US-893 exists to catch, on the product it does not cover. Needs its own reconciliation pass and probably a migration. AC5 OPEN AND PRE-EXISTING - the resync remedy in admin-billing.ts (pickRelevantSubscription) lists by customer with no product filter. Destructive, and it predates every buyer row I wrote; namespacing removes the most likely TRIGGER but not the hazard itself. ALSO SURFACED BY THE SAME SWEEP, recorded here rather than lost: no admin route reads buyer_plan / buyer_subscription_status at all, so support cannot see, cancel, change or comp a buyer subscription, and buyer past-due accounts never enter the operator dunning queue. Buyer refunds DO work, because charges are listed customer-wide. Account export and deletion are correctly covered (buyer columns via select *, buyer tables via BUYER_PII_TABLES, subscription cancelled by the customer delete). The trial-expiry and journey crons are correctly seller-only because no buyer trial exists. VERIFIED: deno check clean on webhooks.ts, payments.ts and billing-reconciliation.ts; deno lint clean across 1493 files; buyer-audit-namespace_test.ts 5 passed (new); full edge suite 6496 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 5). | 2026-08-10 AC5 DONE. I called this 'not agent work' in the previous pass and that was wrong - the fix is a product filter, which is code. Correcting it here rather than leaving the misjudgement standing. THE DEFECT, and it is pre-existing rather than mine: the resync fallback listed the customer's subscriptions with NO product filter, and buyer and seller subscriptions ride the SAME Stripe customer. So for a buyer-only account - or a seller whose own subscription had lapsed - pickRelevantSubscription returned the BUYER subscription and the resync wrote its id into flipdesk_subscription_id, its status into subscription_status, and mapSubscriptionToFlipdeskPlan(buyerSub) ?? 'free' into flipdesk_plan. The row then claims an ACTIVE subscription on a FREE plan, pointing at the other product's. THE SECOND-ORDER DAMAGE IS WHAT MAKES IT URGENT. POST /users/:id/change-plan acts on flipdesk_subscription_id. So support changing that person's FlipDesk plan afterwards would push a FlipDesk PRICE onto their Guard or Connoisseur subscription - a real charge, on the wrong product, initiated by someone trying to help. That is the chain the previous pass described and did not close. FIXED IN TWO PLACES, because one alone leaves the corruption alive. (1) pickRelevantSubscription filters buyer subscriptions out BEFORE the live/newest pick, and returns null when every candidate is a buyer one - null is the correct answer, since the caller then records 'no seller subscription', which is true; borrowing the other product's is what created the defect. (2) THE REPAIR HALF: if the STORED flipdesk_subscription_id already points at a buyer subscription - which an earlier unfiltered resync could have written - the retrieve path now discards it and falls through to the (now filtered) customer lookup, so the run CORRECTS the row instead of resyncing the seller columns from the buyer's state forever. Without that, the retrieve short-circuits the lookup and the corruption is permanent. THE TESTS PIN THE FILTER'S COMPLETENESS, not its presence: a filter applied to the candidate list while `live` is still picked from the unfiltered one would return a buyer subscription about half the time and read as fixed. Every subsequent read must be off the filtered list, and two assertions fail if `subs.find(` or `[...subs]` survives anywhere in the function. A fourth case pins the blast radius - the seller resync must write no buyer_* column, because buyer state is owned by customer.subscription.updated and this route has no buyer reconciliation behind it. SIX SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the filter removed, the live pick reading the unfiltered list, the newest-fallback reading the unfiltered list, the all-buyer case falling back instead of returning null, the stored-buyer-id guard removed, and the resync starting to write buyer columns. AC4 REMAINS THE ONLY OPEN ONE and it genuinely is not a filter: buyer subscriptions are not reconciled at all, because CachedSubscriptionState has no buyer columns and the 00217 RPC selects none. A dropped buyer webhook still drifts permanently with nothing detecting it. That needs its own reconciliation pass and probably a migration to widen the RPC. VERIFIED: deno check clean on admin-billing.ts; deno lint clean across 1494 files; resync-product-filter_test.ts 4 passed (new); full edge suite 6500 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 4). | 2026-08-10 THE OTHER END OF THE SAME FALSE FLAG, which AC5 alone did not close. jobs-billing-reconciliation.ts fetchStripeSubscriptions builds a map of every live Stripe subscription KEYED BY CUSTOMER, and detectStripeDivergence compares it against the SELLER cached columns. Buyer and seller subscriptions share one customer, and the map was unfiltered - so an account holding an active Guard plan and a canceled FlipDesk one produced a stripe_divergence flag claiming Stripe thinks they are active. THE TWO DEFECTS FED EACH OTHER: this manufactured the flag, and the resync fixed in the previous pass was the remedy that flag points at - the one that adopted the buyer subscription into flipdesk_subscription_id. Fixing only the resync would have left the queue generating the cases; fixing only the sweep would have left the button loaded. Both halves are now filtered by the same predicate. THE FILTER IS NOT A TIDY-UP, and a second test says so: `status: "all"` stays, because 'Stripe says canceled while we say active' is the most expensive divergence there is - a customer served a paid plan for free - and narrowing the list is exactly what would hide it. The prefer-live-over-canceled rule is pinned too. ⚠ THE SHARED SOURCE-SCAN HELPER HAD A SECOND BUG, found by these tests failing against CORRECT code. fnBody took the first `{` after the parameter list - but a RETURN TYPE can contain one: fetchStripeSubscriptions is declared `): Promise<Map<string, { id: string; status: string | null }> | null> {`. So the 'body' was the return type annotation and two true assertions failed as though the code were missing. This is the SECOND instance of the same class in that helper (the first was an inline object PARAMETER type), and both look identical from the test - which makes the tempting response 'weaken the assertion' rather than 'fix the slicer'. fnBody now tracks angle-bracket depth and takes the first brace outside it. Two new fixtures in source-scan_test.ts cover the return type and a generic parameter list. That is exactly why US-2454 gave the helper its own tests an hour ago: the primitive is used by nine guards now, and a slicing bug in it silently weakens all of them at once. FOUR SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the sweep no longer filtering, the filter moved AFTER the map write, `status: "all"` removed, and fnBody reverted to the naive brace search - which correctly reddens the two sweep tests AND its own new fixture, because that is what a broken primitive does. ⚠ ONE MUTATION PROVED NOTHING FIRST TIME, third occurrence today: my 'filter after write' edit put the set AFTER the filter anyway, so it tested nothing. Re-anchored so the write genuinely precedes the filter. A sabotage that does not create the condition it names is a green run that means nothing. AC4 REMAINS OPEN and is now the only one. Buyer subscriptions are still not reconciled at all - CachedSubscriptionState has no buyer columns, the 00217 RPC selects none, and billing_reconciliation_flags is keyed one-open-flag-per-user with no product dimension, so a buyer flag and a seller flag cannot coexist. That last point is why AC4 genuinely needs a migration rather than another filter, and it is the reason I am not starting it in the same breath as two held prod changes. VERIFIED: deno check clean on jobs-billing-reconciliation.ts; deno lint clean across 1494 files; resync-product-filter_test.ts 6 passed (2 new) and source-scan_test.ts 12 passed (2 new); full edge suite 6504 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 4). | 2026-08-10 THE PATTERN IS NOW WRITTEN DOWN. Ten defects in one session shared one sentence, and nothing recorded it — so instance eleven was going to be written by whoever touches the seller subscription next. NEW vault/70-agent/buyer-is-a-second-tenant.md. All ten in a table with what a buyer actually got, plus the two one level up (buyer audit rows read as seller signals; no admin surface reading a buyer column). THE PART WORTH THE NOTE IS WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING, because it is not carelessness. The early return is USUALLY CORRECT: `if (invoiceIsBuyer(invoice)) return;` genuinely guards the seller cycle resets, the dunning transition and the plan columns. The bug is never the return - it is that something which was NOT seller-specific had been written inside the region the return protects. So a reviewer sees a guard with a good reason, and the reason is true. AND THE COMMENTS MADE IT WORSE, twice. One skip read 'so a buyer doesn't get a seller-shaped email' - an honest statement of intent whose consequence, silence, nobody re-read. Another said the buyer path 'is carried by subscription.updated', which is true of the STATUS and false of the EMAIL three lines below it. Both read as decisions. THE THIRD REASON IS THE ONE I WOULD NOT HAVE GUESSED: half a feature working hides the other half. Buyer CHARGES show in the admin tools, because charges are listed customer-wide - so the money half of a support call worked while the state half was blank. A gap that breaks half a workflow is a gap nobody reports, because the half that works is the half people phone about. SIX-POINT CHECKLIST for anyone touching the seller subscription, each earned from a specific defect: does the buyer equivalent EXIST (name the file); what sits BELOW an early return that is not seller-specific; split the send out rather than widening the skip (threading isBuyer past every write is how a buyer's renewal resets a seller's quota); product is a PARAMETER, never inferred; is the SENTENCE true of the buyer product; and does the guard name a route or find them. PLUS THE ENUM TRAP, which caught me four separate times: from_plan/to_plan are typed public.flipdesk_plan (00037) and buyer tiers are public.buyer_plan (00402), so writing 'guard' raises 22P02 - and every one of those inserts is best-effort by design, so the row silently never appears while the charge goes through. ALSO CLEARED THE VAULT WARNING I had been leaving deliberately. vault/50-business/ios-in-app-purchases.md drifted against appstore.ts and I had refused to bump 'reviewed' without a genuine re-read, since doing that to silence a warning is the one failure no automation catches. Re-read it properly and found a sentence that HAD gone stale: 'a user who subscribes on both web and iOS is currently only caught by hand'. US-2456 closed that at purchase time on every path. Corrected the sentence, added precedence.ts to its code_refs, and bumped the date on the strength of an actual read rather than to clear a line. VERIFIED: vault:lint --strict clean at 169 notes, zero warnings for the first time today. | 2026-08-10 AC4 SCOPED IN FULL AND DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT. The reasoning matters more than the plan, so it is first. WHY NOT NOW: there is already ONE migration in the queue (00586) that has never been executed against a Postgres, because Docker is down and verify:db cannot boot the throwaway stack. AC4 needs a SECOND migration - larger, and it alters a UNIQUE INDEX on an operator-facing table. Adding an untested index change on top of an untested function replacement is compounding, and it gates the push on two prod applies instead of one. This is the same call US-2118 made about the proration figures: when the verification that would catch a mistake is unavailable, shipping the mistake-prone half is worse than waiting. Re-check `docker info`; if it is up, this is a single focused session. THE BLOCKER IS MEASURED, not assumed. billing_reconciliation_flags (00217) carries a partial UNIQUE INDEX billing_reconciliation_flags_open_subject_key ON (subject_user_id) WHERE status = 'open'. ONE open flag per person, with no column saying which product it is about. So a buyer flag and a seller flag cannot coexist for the same customer, and the job would silently overwrite one with the other - which is worse than not reconciling buyers at all, because it would start LOSING seller flags. That index is why this cannot be done with a filter. THE PLAN, in the order it has to happen: (1) MIGRATION. ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS product text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'flipdesk' (the default is what makes it safe on a table with live rows - every existing flag IS a seller flag). DROP the partial unique index and recreate it on (subject_user_id, product) WHERE status='open'. Then CREATE OR REPLACE reconciliation_candidates to return buyer_status, buyer_plan and buyer_subscription_id alongside the seller columns, and to stop filtering the event scan to seller rows only - it must return the latest SELLER event and the latest BUYER event per user, which with the US-2457 namespacing is now a clean split on event_type LIKE 'buyer.%'. US-1108 triple: idempotent, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in the same commit, self-record footer, manifest regenerated. (2) lib/billing-reconciliation.ts. CachedSubscriptionState gains a buyer variant rather than being widened - the same argument the precedence helpers settled in US-2456, and for the same reason: a type that accepts either row family is how a comparison ends up reading the wrong one. detectDivergence's buyer short-circuit (added today) is REPLACED by a real buyer comparison, and that is the line to be careful about - until the migration lands, the skip is what stops false flags. (3) THE JOB. fetchStripeSubscriptions currently filters buyer subscriptions OUT and keys by customer. For the buyer half it needs the opposite selection, keyed the same way - which means the map must become two maps, or one keyed by (customer, product). Do NOT reuse the seller map; it is the shape that caused this story. (4) SIX CONSUMERS to update, enumerated so none is missed: admin-billing.ts at 1470, 1481, 1667 and 1755, lib/agent-tools.ts at 455, and lib/finance-agent.ts. Each currently assumes a flag is about the seller subscription. The two admin panels also need the product on screen - a flag an operator cannot attribute to a product is a flag they cannot act on, and the resync they would reach for is seller-only (AC5). (5) THE RESYNC REMEDY needs a buyer equivalent, or the buyer flags have no fix button. AC5 fixed the seller one so it can no longer ADOPT the buyer subscription; it still cannot RESYNC one. WHAT I WOULD GET WRONG WITHOUT A DATABASE: the index swap. DROP INDEX then CREATE UNIQUE INDEX on a table with existing rows fails if any two open flags for one subject would now collide - they cannot today, since every row is implicitly seller, but that is exactly the assumption a throwaway-stack run exists to prove rather than reason about. STATUS: AC1, AC2, AC3 and AC5 are done and committed. AC4 is the only one left and it is one focused session behind a working Docker.

userStories.title: Support cannot see a buyer subscription at all — no admin route reads buyer_plan or buyer_subscription_status
userStories.description: Found 2026-08-10 by a sweep for buyer/seller asymmetries. Not one admin route reads buyer_plan, buyer_subscription_status or buyer_subscription_id. admin-growth exposes an aggregate buyer rollup and nothing per-account. Concretely: GET /users/:id/payments (admin-billing.ts) selects only flipdesk_subscription_id, so an agent opening a Guard or Connoisseur subscriber sees subscription: null and has no way to tell whether they are subscribed, on what, or when it renews. POST /users/:id/change-plan acts solely on flipdesk_subscription_id, so there is no admin path to cancel, downgrade or change a buyer subscription. admin-users POST /:id/plan writes flipdesk_plan and subscription_status, so a buyer comp or goodwill grant is impossible. And the operator dunning queue filters users.subscription_status, so a buyer whose card is failing never appears in it. Buyer REFUNDS do work, because charges are listed customer-wide and both subscriptions ride one Stripe customer — which makes the gap easy to miss, since the money half of a support conversation succeeds while the state half shows nothing.
acceptanceCriteria: GET /users/:id/payments returns the buyer subscription alongside the seller one, each labelled with its product, so an agent can see what the customer actually holds.

The response shape is additive: the existing `subscription` field keeps its exact meaning (the seller subscription) so the admin UI and any consumer are unchanged, and the buyer state arrives beside it rather than replacing it.
A test asserts the two are never conflated — a buyer-only account must not report its buyer subscription in the seller field, which is the same mistake the reconciliation resync made (US-2457 AC5).

OPEN / NEEDS A DECISION: whether support should be able to CANCEL or CHANGE a buyer subscription, and whether a buyer comp is a product we want. Both are writes against a customer's money and neither is a read-only fix; the comp path also needs a buyer equivalent of subscription_status='comp', which today is a seller-only enum value.

OPEN / NEEDS A MIGRATION: buyer past-due accounts in the operator dunning queue. The panel filters users.subscription_status, and there is no buyer_past_due_since column, so the US-395 grace clock has no buyer equivalent to sort by.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-10 AC1, AC2 and AC3 DONE. AC4 and AC5 stay open by design - one needs a product decision, the other a migration - and they are named here so the sweep that found them is not lost. GET /users/:id/payments now returns buyerSubscription beside subscription. Before this, an agent opening a Guard or Connoisseur subscriber saw subscription: null and had no way to tell whether they were subscribed, to what, or when it renewed. WHY IT WENT UNNOTICED, and it is the interesting part: the CHARGES were fine. They are listed customer-wide and both products ride one Stripe customer, so the money half of a support conversation worked - an agent could see the payments and refund them - while the state half was blank. A gap that only breaks half of a workflow is a gap nobody reports, because the half that works is the half people call about. AC2 IS ADDITIVE ON PURPOSE. `subscription` keeps its exact meaning, the SELLER subscription, so the admin UI and every other consumer are untouched. Repurposing it to 'whichever they have' would have been fewer lines and would have repeated the exact conflation US-2457 spent two commits undoing. The no-customer early return carries buyerSubscription: null too, so a caller never gets undefined on one path and null on the other - a test pins that, because it is the kind of asymmetry that shows up as a crash six months later. AC3: each subscription is retrieved by its OWN stored id. Listing the customer and choosing is precisely what let the reconciliation resync adopt the buyer subscription into the seller columns; the two ids are recorded separately so nobody has to guess, and a test fails if this route ever calls subscriptions.list. BOTH SUMMARIES GO THROUGH ONE SHARED SHAPE, extracted rather than copied. The agent is comparing one against the other, and two hand-written shapes drift - the drift shows up as a field present for sellers and missing for buyers, which reads as 'the buyer has no renewal date' rather than as a bug. SIX SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening its own case: the buyer field dropped from the response, buyer_subscription_id dropped from the SELECT, the seller field repurposed, the early return forgetting the new field, the buyer sub picked off the customer list, and the shared summary losing the renewal date. ONE ASSERTION WAS TOO LOOSE AND SABOTAGE CAUGHT IT - the fourth time today for this exact shape. I checked that buyer_subscription_id appears in the ROUTE; it also appears in the retrieve below, so dropping it from the SELECT stayed green. An unselected column is undefined, the retrieve is skipped, and the agent sees the same blank as before with no error anywhere. Now scoped to the select list itself. AC4 OPEN - a product decision, not a build. Whether support may CANCEL or CHANGE a buyer subscription is a write against a customer's money, and a buyer comp additionally needs a buyer equivalent of subscription_status='comp', which today is a seller-only enum value. AC5 OPEN - needs a migration. Buyer past-due accounts cannot enter the operator dunning queue: the panel filters users.subscription_status, and there is no buyer_past_due_since column, so the US-395 grace clock has no buyer equivalent to sort by. VERIFIED: deno check clean on admin-billing.ts; deno lint clean across 1495 files; admin-buyer-visibility_test.ts 4 passed (new); full edge suite 6508 passed / 0 failed / 176 ignored (up 4). | 2026-08-10 (second pass) I SHIPPED THE API FIELD AND NOTHING RENDERED IT. Correcting my own instance of the exact failure this session keeps finding in other people's work. The previous commit added buyerSubscription to GET /users/:id/payments and stopped. src/components/admin/billing-actions-card.tsx - the only consumer - typed and rendered `subscription` alone, so support still saw nothing for a buyer subscriber. A field with no surface is invisible to tsc, to lint, and to every test that exercises the route directly, which is precisely how US-2145's contest endpoint sat unreachable behind a missing button and how confirm-signup corroborated a row that was never written. FIXED: both subscriptions now render, each through one shared SubscriptionSummary block and each LABELLED by product. The label is a required prop rather than defaulted - two subscriptions can be on screen at once and the agent is about to act on whichever they believe they are looking at, so an unlabelled one is worse than none. A test asserts the render, the label, and that both go through the shared block, so a field cannot appear for the seller and not the buyer. ⚠ AND A GENUINELY SURPRISING SIDE EFFECT, worth recording because nothing warns you about it. Extracting the shared mapper as a top-level `function` in admin-billing.ts made THREE UNRELATED ROUTES fail the US-2355 audit-policy guard - /pending-refunds/:id/resolve, /webhook-dead-letters/:id/resolve and the reconciliation resync all reported as writing no audit row. They audit fine. scripts/audit-admin-mutations.mjs classifies a route by appending the body of any TOP-LEVEL DECLARATION it references, and declarations() slices each declaration's body from itself to THE NEXT DECLARATION IN THE FILE. Adding one anywhere moves those boundaries, so a purely presentational helper silently changed the audit classification of routes it has nothing to do with. RESOLVED BY MOVING THE MAPPER TO lib/admin-subscription-summary.ts, with the reason in its header so nobody moves it back for tidiness. That is the right home anyway - it is a pure Stripe-to-view mapper with no route concerns - but the forcing reason is the classifier, and a future reader would never guess it. I DID NOT WEAKEN THE CLASSIFIER, which was the tempting alternative: its slicing model is genuinely fragile, but loosening a guard that decides 'is this admin action audited' to unblock a cosmetic refactor is the worst possible trade. Recorded here instead; if it bites again it deserves its own story rather than an exemption. THREE SABOTAGE MUTATIONS, each reddening the render guard: the buyer block never rendered (the state I shipped an hour ago), the labels dropped so an agent cannot tell the two apart, and the buyer block hand-written instead of sharing the seller's. VERIFIED: npx tsc -b clean; eslint 0 errors / 13 warnings; ui:check 0 blocking; deno lint clean across 1496 files; admin-buyer-visibility_test.ts 5 passed (1 new); admin-audit-policy.test.ts 6 passed (restored); full edge suite 6509 passed / 0 failed; full web suite 3937 passed / 0 failed across 322 files.

userStories.description: As the grading pipeline, we want the prompt hints and macro-quality floors to speak in roles, so the model is told what a photo shows rather than which numbered slot it landed in.
acceptanceCriteria: PREREQUISITE, found 2026-08-11: the role has to REACH the grader first. submission_images.image_type is a Postgres ENUM (00001, grown by 00103), so a role cannot be encoded into it and the epic deliberately stopped growing that enum - this needs a submission_images.image_role column plus mapPhotoTypeForGrading taking the (type, role) pair. Load the `migrations` skill; it is a US-1108 triple
ai-grading.ts, ai-authenticity.ts and ai-extract.ts prompt hints name roles (fabric, hem, hardware, brand, size, care) instead of detail_2 / detail_3 / detail_4 / tag_2
macro-photo-quality.ts resolution and sharpness floors move from per-numbered-slot to per-role, keeping today's numbers for the equivalent role
ai-extract is told WHICH tag photo carries the brand and which carries the size, instead of guessing between tag and tag_2
No change to the fabric-close-up confidence cap logic, which already moved to roles in US-2467
userStories.notes: [P1][FlipDesk/Photos] Category-aware photo tags epic (US-2461). SPLIT OUT OF US-2467 on 2026-08-10. 2026-08-11 IN PROGRESS - AC1/AC3/AC4 done, AC2 built but gated, AC5 verified untouched. AC1 (the prereq) is DONE: migration 00589 adds submission_images.image_role (US-1108 triple; HELD - see PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md, do NOT push before Dj applies it), and mapPhotoTypeForGrading now takes the (type, role) pair and returns {imageType, imageRole}. THAT FIXED A LIVE REGRESSION nobody had reported: 00587 rewrote measurement_chest into (measurement, chest), a bare measurement is the MeasureCard calibration frame that 00346 excludes from grading on purpose, and the function read the type alone - so from 00587 onward EVERY tape-measure photo resolved to null and silently stopped reaching the grader. Two cases in grading-readiness-parity_test.ts pin it, and it is written into vault/20-domain/listing-photos.md, which already carried the identical warning for LISTABILITY and had never had it applied to grading. AC3 DONE: macro-photo-quality.ts keys every floor on (type, role) via baseSlot(); the retired numbered slots collapse onto their base pair so an older cached bundle still resolves; the guidance copy names the role (fill the frame with the fabric close-up). The numbers did NOT move - MACRO_MIN_LONG_EDGE_BY_ROLE ships deliberately EMPTY, because raising detail:fabric is an accuracy change that belongs behind an eval, not inside a refactor whose whole claim is that nothing moved. Also closed a latent gap: RETIRED_PHOTO_TYPES is the FlipDesk vocabulary only, so the grading spelling label_2 needed its own collapse or the both-spellings test would have gone red. AC4 DONE and LIVE: ai-extract is an unversioned prompt, so it ships without a gate. ExtractPhoto carries a role, photoSlotLabel() announces Photo 3 (tag: size tag) instead of Photo 3 (tag), the guidance line names which role holds brand / size / care / made-in, and flipdesk-ai.ts selects photo_role. AC2 BUILT BUT NOT LIVE, and that is the correct state: a grading prompt only changes through shadow to eval gate to canary. IMAGE_ROLE_CONTEXT covers 15 (image_type, role) pairs; buildUserPrompt and analyzeImage take imageRole as a LAST positional param; grading-pipeline selects image_role and passes it; PerImageAnalysis carries image_role; the composite stamps a +roles suffix (appended after +cat2) only when a role actually SELECTED a sentence. All of it behind GRADING_PHOTO_ROLES, default off and fail-closed, with photo-role-prompts_test.ts pinning byte-identity when off. Same shape and same reasoning as GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 (US-2222). ai-authenticity turned out to have NO numbered-slot prompt hints at all - its only slot-number references are AUTHENTICITY_IMAGE_PRIORITY. So selectAuthenticityImages now ranks detail:hardware / hem / collar / print / fabric above a bare detail, using fractional ranks so a role can never displace serial or marking (US-2134 ordering stands). MACRO_EVIDENCE_TYPES was left alone on purpose: it gates a confidence cap, and widening it would RAISE authenticity confidence on existing submissions. WHAT IS LEFT is an operator action: apply 00589 to prod, then run the golden-set eval with GRADING_PHOTO_ROLES on and take it through a canary slice before flipping it in prod. Both need real vision calls, so neither CI nor an agent can do them.
